title: ‘Rojo’ Director Benjamín Naishtat on Awaited Toronto, San Sebastián Title ‘Glaxo,’ the Impunity of Power and Connecting via Genre
full_text: Sep 11, 2026 6:25am PT ‘Rojo’ Director Benjamín Naishtat on Awaited Toronto, San Sebastián Title ‘Glaxo,’ the Impunity of Power and Connecting via Genre Noting that ‘Glaxo,’ from São Paulo-based RT Features and Rei Pictures in Buenos Aires, is set entirely in Argentina but shot in Brazil, Naishtat laments: Argentina is 'a country with a great filmmaking tradition and it is now in very serious danger' By John Hopewell , Roberto Prieto Lali Espósito in 'Glaxo' Courtesy of RT Features, Rei Pictures “At what precise moment had Peru fucked itself up?” Nobel Prize winning author Mario Vargas Llosa famously asks at the beginning of “Conversation at The Cathedral.” In “ Glaxo ,” one of the most awaited of Latin American films this year, director Benjamín Naishtat charts what he describes as the whole of Argentina’s loss of innocence, which again has its origins in 1950s dictatorship and is equally pervasive. Related Stories 'The Whisper Man' Review: Diverting Netflix Serial Killer Chiller Doesn't Demand Much of Robert De Niro After the lighter turn of co-directing “Puán,” a “deliciously droll” makeover movie, said Variety , in “Glaxo,” which world premieres in Toronto’s Special Presentations, Naishtat returns to the disturbing collective psychology portrait of “Rojo,” charting the impunity of power — a cop, and the Glaxo corporation — and a tale of betrayals in its central coming of age section. Popular on Variety Set along three timelines — Florida, outside Buenos Aires, on June 6, 1956, and then Chivilcoy, a town in the sticks also outside the Argentine capital one year later and then in 1984. Esteban Bigliardi as Flaco in ‘Glaxo’ Courtesy of RT Features, Rei Pictures In the first, with Argentina under military dictatorship, based on historical facts depicted by Argentine writer Roberto Walsh in a trailblazing example of a non-fiction novel — police commissioner Folcada arrests 12 men listening to a boxing match, and then is leaned on by his boss to make an example of them. One year later, now a civilian and a wealthy ranch owner, Folcada has moved to Chivilcoy with his stunning wife, Negra Morcada (Lali Espósito, notable), dazzling four teen friends — Miguelito, Verdemann, “Bicho” and Lucio. “This is the story of a betrayal,” says narrator Miguelito. In fact it’s the story of multiple endemic betrayals driven by the exercise of unaccountable power and the misjudgment of adolescence, under the weight of which four teens’ seemingly “Stand by Me” friendship unravels. If “Rojo” was a “witheringly provocative examination of temporary moral eclipse becoming permanent moral apocalypse,” as Variety noted , “Glaxo” delivers a broader historical take on the same Argentinean dark ages. It delivers a pedigree producer package as a production of Brazil’s RT Features (“Paper Tiger,” “I’m Still Here”), produced by Argentina’s Rei Pictures (“Zama,” “The Settlers”). The film is inspired by novel “Glaxo,” from the film’s co-writer, Hernán Ronsino, which was partly inspired in turn by Walsh’s “Operation Masacre.” This deep concern for heritage – historical, literary, cinematographic – is one of the film’s sources of emotion. Variety talked to Naishtat before the Toronto world premiere of “Glaxo,” after which the film segues for its European bow in main competition at San Sebastián. Two first questions. At the beginning of the “Conversation in The Cathedral,” Mario Vargas Llosa famously asks: “At what precise moment had Peru fucked itself up?” It seems that to a certain extent Hernán Ronsino and you in “Glaxo” are asking the same question about Argentina. Also Miguelito, the narrator, says “This is the story of a betrayal. It seems to me that this is the story of many betrayals…. Benjamin Naishtat : I think that’s a very good analysis of the film, and basically this reading is obviously connected to Hernán Ronsino’s novel. When I read the novel for the first time, two things struck me. First, its very austere style, almost like an American police crime novel, but also closely related to Argentine writer Rodolfo Walsh, the author of “Operation Massacre,” a book that has a strong connection to “Glaxo.” The film “Glaxo· also has a string connection to “Operation Massacre,” an underground film from 1973 by Jorge Cedrón, a filmmaker who isn’t very well known but who is very important in the mysterious history of Argentine cinema. I wanted to mention that because it’s important. But going back to your point, yes, I think it really is an open question for the audience. To what extent does “Glaxo” suggest any answers? Naishtat: I don’t think the film tries to give us an answer but it simply presents us with the question. As an audience member, I’m more interested in leaving with more questions than with simple answers. That’s what we tried to do with this project: generate questions in a historical echo going backwards, but posing possible hypotheses about when Argentina got screwed and also about Argentina’s present. I think we tried to analyze the current state of Argentina from a different angle and from a different perspective. One possible hypothesis comes in the prologue, set on June 9, 1956, turning on Police Commissioner Folcada, which suggests the terrible impunity of power. The other might be the terribly limited prospects of people like Miguelito living in Chivilcoy, a town outside Buenos Aires, where the two latter parts of the film is set. Naishtat: The impunity of power is a good point. It relates to your earlier question and is a good starting point in relation to what impunity means in Argentina. In fact, the historical episodes depicted in the prologue — historical episodes that occurred in 1956 — remain unpunished to this day. Those responsible for that massacre never had to pay a price for what they did. Regarding Miguelito and his life opportunities, I do share your view, but it’s also related to the film being not only a thriller but melodrama and also a coming-of-age story. I personally love the coming-of-age genre. What’s fascinating is that it connects you to an age we’ve all lived through — adolescence — in which love, and even more so, falling in love, has a devastating power over you. Without knowing who we are, we already have the capacity to fall in love in a way that we will never again experience. And that’s dangerous. So I tried to play with those themes a little bit by telling a story about adolescent love. You’ve mentioned genres. The film plays with their different registers and has multiple echoes from other films. Naishtat: This is my second collaboration after “Rojo.” with cinematographer Pedro Sotero. “Rojo” was a language exercise in relation to thrillers and television from the ‘70s. “Glaxo” has three different languages in the same film. So we have a prologue, which relates to clandestine Latin American films from the ‘70s, filmed as if it was shot on Super 16mm, with texture, like using only a single lens, and with very precarious shooting and lighting conditions. Courtesy of RT Features, Rei Pictures Then we have the main 1950s section, which tries to play with Italian and American melodrama, like films such as “A Place in the Sun” or “Giant” by George Stevens, which were strong points of reference for the images in that section. Then we have the film-noir section set in the 1980s, shot in CinemaScope with anamorphic lenses to generate maximum atmosphere, which honestly, was a lot of fun. We’re both huge cinephiles. Pedro and I love genre cinema, and I think we’re convinced that the future of cinema, if there is one, is a popular future, let’s say within the popular genres — being able to talk to the audience and bring complexity to popular genres. In other words, recovering the complexity that popular genres used to have in other eras. The credits say that “Glaxo” is a production of Brazil’s RT Features produced by Argentina’s Rei Pictures. That speaks volumes of the comparative current state of the two countries’ film industries. Naishtat : Yes. This is very important. As the film’s credits say, the producer of the film is Rodrigo Teixeira and his Brazilian production company RT Features and Rei Pictures is a minority co-producer on the Argentine side. The film was shot entirely in Brazil, which is very strange, because it’s set entirely in Argentina and so it was a very difficult decision for me. Rodrigo and I wanted to shoot it in Argentina, but the current state of Argentina made that impossible. The cuts and the freezing of public funding for the film industry have been brutal for Argentine cinema. There are fewer productions now and less of a presence in the major markets and the major festivals. And perhaps what will become even more evident in the coming years will be the total lack of promoting new talent and new voices. There used to be a very interesting generation making their first features not only in Buenos Aires, but in Córdoba, in other cities, in Patagonia — genuinely interesting voices. This government, which is waging an open war on culture in general, is, in my opinion, a fascist government, an enemy of culture, one that has no cultural politics whatsoever. It doesn’t even have conservative politics, it has no politics at all; the politics is that there are no cultural politics and this is derailing the life plans of many people. I personally can keep working because, as you know, this is my fifth film and I’ve been able to secure financing in Brazil with Rodrigo Teixeira, or in France, or in other places. But if I had to start my career today, I’d have to work somewhere else. I wouldn’t be able to work in cinema, and this is what’s happening in Argentina, which is very sad. I think it’s important to call this out, because as you know, we’re a country with a great filmmaking tradition and it is now in very serious danger. ‘Shark Tank India’ Sets Season 6 With Parrot Campaign on SonyLIV (EXCLUSIVE) Hansal Mehta, Siddharth Bodke on ‘Scam 2010’ as First Look Unveiled for SonyLIV Series: ‘A Story About Ambition, Influence and Arrogance’ (EXCLUSIVE) Loading comments... title: ‘R.L. Stine’s Pumpkinhead 2’ Launches At TIFF Market, Details Revealed With Cassandra Peterson AKA ‘Elvira Mistress Of The Dark’ Joining Cast
full_text: Skip to main content By Andreas Wiseman Andreas Wiseman Executive Editor, Film & International @AndreasWiseman More Stories By Andreas Zurich Summit: Edward Berger, Robbie Brenner, Oliver Berben, Janine Jackowski, Martin Moszkowicz & More Join Swiss Conference Lineup Noah Schnapp, David Mazouz & Seu Jorge Leading Thriller ‘Stealing From Pablo’; Myriad Launching For TIFF Market Odeya Rush, Annarah Cymone & Neela Jolene Join Justin Long & Iris Apatow In Killer Bee Movie ‘Stung’, Filming Wraps View All September 11, 2026 6:17am 'Pumpkinhead 2;' Cassandra Peterson EXCLUSIVE : Blue Fox Entertainment will launch international sales at the TIFF market to R.L. Stine’s Pumpkinhead 2 , the upcoming Tubi Original sequel to the young-adult horror film R.L. Stine’s Pumpkinhead . Written and directed by Jem Garrard, who also helmed the original R.L. Stine’s Pumpkinhead , the sequel continues author Stine’s Pumpkinhead story. The synopsis reads: “When a new Pumpkinhead curse awakens in Redhaven, Sam and Becka must stop it before it claims the entire town.” Bean Reid, Adeline Lo and Matty Finochio return to star in the sequel, with additional casting due to be announced at a later date. Joining the returning cast is Cassandra Peterson, best known as character ‘Elvira, Mistress of the Dark’, who takes on the role of Cassandra, “a wise and ancient witch whose arrival could prove pivotal to the events unfolding in Redhaven”. Related Stories News Justin Trudeau Launching Production Company At TIFF Festivals John Trengove's 'The Smell Of Apples' Sells To France Ahead Of TIFF Debut The film is slated to premiere on Tubi this fall as part of the streamer’s Terror on Tubi horror hub. Pic is produced by Front Street Pictures, the film is executive produced by James Mattagne, Joan Waricha, Harvey Kahn, Yvonne Bernard, Dan Bernard, Jem Garrard, Allen Lewis, and Rama Diallo. Watch on Deadline R.L. Stine’s Pumpkinhead premiered on Tubi in 2025. Inspired by an episode of R.L. Stine’s The Haunting Hour , the film “follows teenager Sam after his brother Finn mysteriously vanishes and everyone in town—including Sam’s mother—seems to have forgotten he ever existed. With Halloween approaching, Sam, his friend Becka and eccentric local Rusty must uncover the truth and break a harvest curse before it is too late.” The original film stars Bean Reid, Adeline Lo, Kevin McNulty, Bob Frazer, Matty Finochio and Seth Isaac Johnson. “R.L. Stine’s stories have been a gateway into horror for generations of young audiences, and Pumpkinhead brings that same spirit of adventure, scares and fun to a new generation,” said Lisa Gutberlet, President of Blue Fox Entertainment, about the Goosebumps writer. “We’re thrilled to continue our relationship with Tubi and bring R.L. Stine’s Pumpkinhead 2 to our international buyers at TIFF. Jem Garrard has created another exciting chapter in the mythology, and we’re looking forward to sharing it with audiences around the world.” The acquisition expands Blue Fox Entertainment’s international sales relationship with Tubi, following multiple collaborations, including Buzzkill starring Siena Agudong and Brec Bassinger, and Aliyah’s Interlude . title: Thailand Bets on Film Tourism to Turn Movie Locations Into Travel Destinations
full_text: Sep 11, 2026 6:15am PT Thailand Bets on Film Tourism to Turn Movie Locations Into Travel Destinations By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest New Zealand Set to Unveil Tri-Nation Indigenous Co-Production Initiative at Toronto (EXCLUSIVE) 30 minutes ago Oscars: Singapore Selects Anthony Chen’s ‘We Are All Strangers’ for International Feature Race 4 hours ago San Sebastian Competition Title ‘Border’ Boards Reel Suspects for Global Sales (EXCLUSIVE) 6 hours ago See All HBO The Tourism Authority of Thailand (TAT) has launched “Amazing Locations: From Scene to Scenic,” a campaign built to convert the country’s rising profile as a filming destination into lasting tourism, as productions ranging from “ The White Lotus ” to “The Challenge” Season 42 continue to draw international attention to Thai locations. TAT deputy governor Nithee Seeprae says the campaign grew out of watching how quickly the “set-jetting” trend has taken hold among travelers who plan trips around what they have seen on screen. Related Stories 'The Whisper Man' Review: Diverting Netflix Serial Killer Chiller Doesn't Demand Much of Robert De Niro TAT frames the push as part of a broader strategy to make Thailand a top-of-mind choice for global productions, pointing to the strength of its local crews, production infrastructure, studio facilities and incentive programs as the pillars of that pitch. The campaign’s specific job, as Seeprae describes it, is to bridge filmmaking and travel: encouraging filmmakers to turn Thailand’s varied landscapes into cinematic backdrops while steering travelers toward the real places they recognize from the screen. Popular on Variety “We have seen firsthand how tangibly it benefits destinations and local communities when a film or series puts a place on screen,” Seeprae says. “It genuinely inspires people to travel, and we have seen that pull firsthand, audiences putting Thailand at the top of their must-visit list simply because they fell in love with it on screen first.” The numbers back up the strategy. Seeprae says the country’s cash rebate program has drawn in upward of 100 foreign productions to date, funneling more than THB20 billion ($608 million) toward Thai crews and local economies. The rebate program itself is administered by Thailand’s Dept. of Tourism rather than TAT, though the agency promotes it as part of the country’s broader pitch to filmmakers. He points to Koh Samui as a case study: after the island appeared in the third season of “The White Lotus,” online interest in the destination jumped 88% and hotel reservations there grew 44%, figures he says have been echoed by titles including “The Hangover Part II” and “Jurassic World: Rebirth.” Recent Thailand shoots also include the Bollywood blockbuster “Dhurandhar,” Sam Raimi’s “Send Help,” the survival sequel “Fall 2: Deadpoint” and “John Rambo.” Seeprae says this year’s push doubles down on undiscovered locations rather than simply revisiting places already familiar to international audiences. He points to Isan provinces such as Nong Khai, Bueng Kan and Ubon Ratchathani, along with Nakhon Si Thammarat in the south, as places with striking scenery and a distinct sense of place that international productions have yet to explore. He cites director Apichatpong Weerasethakul’s body of work as proof that cinema can give an entire region “a place in the world’s imagination.” As part of the campaign, TAT is running trips that bring filmmakers, producers, influencers and cultural figures into these locations along both a B2B track focused on production logistics and a B2C track aimed at travelers. The push comes as Thailand’s production sector matures well beyond service work. Nicholas Simon, founder and producer at Indochina Prods., has watched the local crew base grow from working transportation on shoots to running productions worth well over $100 million. “Crew who were working 15 years ago as transport coordinators are now line producing $100 million projects,” Simon says, pointing to Thai nominees at the Creative Emmys for “The White Lotus” and “ Alien: Earth ,” and a Thai costume designer from “The Creator” who is now a voting member of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences. “Jurassic World: Rebirth” behind the scenes Everett Collection Simon credits “The White Lotus” and “Alien: Earth” with changing how Hollywood sees the country itself, rather than as a stand-in for somewhere else. Those productions, he says, also introduced the industry to Thailand’s art department talent, and “the film incentive has driven a new wave of productions scripted Thailand for Thailand.” Simon adds that under-filmed regions such as Songkla, Ranong and the natural rock formations of the north and northeast still hold plenty of unexplored ground, noting that “The Creator” alone shot across 17 of Thailand’s 76 provinces. That maturity has pushed Indochina into original content through its new venture, TSixtySix. Producer Cod Satrusayang, head of studio at TSixtySix, says, “We think given the right support and the right stories, Thailand can become the next Asian wave following in the footsteps of South Korea,“ adding that clients who once came to Thailand purely for service work are increasingly asking about local stories too. Satrusayang says the biggest remaining gap is screenwriting talent able to work within structure, and that streamers willing to back genres beyond horror and romance are reshaping what gets developed. TSixtySix has a heist film releasing early next year and a coming-of-age drama shooting in late January, with Satrusayang predicting demand for Thai content will keep rising. The country’s reputation as a source of acclaimed auteurs reinforces its appeal as a location, according to Raymond Phathanavirangoon, producer and founder of the SEAFIC Script Lab. Wong Kar Wai shot much of “In the Mood for Love” in Thailand because, Phathanavirangoon says, “there are locations in Thailand that seem untouched by time since the 1950s-1960s.” He notes that European filmmakers have told him Bangkok’s futuristic skyline could support a science-fiction film in the vein of “Alphaville,” and points to the local production “A Useful Ghost” as an example of a film built around unusual local settings. Phathanavirangoon says specificity, not international polish, is what makes Thai stories travel, citing “9 Temples to Heaven” and the Burmese Busan winner “Ma — Cry of Silence” as films that succeeded by staying rooted in local culture rather than chasing a global audience. Phathanavirangoon says independent filmmakers are often the ones expanding what audiences associate with Thailand beyond its best-known landmarks. He points to Udon Thani, near the Phu Phra Bat Historical Park, and a growing contemporary arts scene anchored by museums such as Dib and MAIIAM, as the kind of settings independent directors are now drawing on. Director Chantana Tiprachart’s upcoming “Esarn Seven,” shot north of Udon Thani, is one example he cites of a film built around a region rarely seen on screen. Producer Cattleya Paosrijarern, whose work centers on independent and auteur cinema, says international shoots and homegrown storytelling can coexist without one undermining the other. “Even with line production, we always push to be creative partners, not just vendors,” Paosrijarern says. She says international funding is welcome but “the money must serve the artist’s vision,” and argues that hyper-local Thai stories only resonate abroad “when it’s backed by quality,” pointing to knowledge, vision and sustained policy support as the real drivers of that continuity. Her upcoming slate includes “Tremble Like a Flower,” the debut feature from visual artist Pathompon Tesprateep, and “Esarn Seven.” Thailand’s location appeal extends into unscripted television. “The Challenge” Season 42 shot across Bangkok, Pattaya and the Chonburi region, and executive producer Justin Booth says the decision came down to more than scenery. “Thailand has some of the most professional and polished art department personnel anywhere in the world, and you’re able to access that level of talent at a better price,” Booth says. He adds that the range of environments within a compact area gave producers flexibility to design challenges they could not have built elsewhere, comparing the local infrastructure favorably with other countries that have hosted the franchise. Season 42 also splits its 24 competitors into three teams competing for a share of $500,000, reviving the “Cutthroat” format the show first used in 2009. Booth says the cast made the timing right for the format’s return, and that viewers should watch how team dynamics evolve after a run of seasons built around pairs and individual competition. Asked whether he’s conscious that viewers might want to visit places the show has featured, Booth says that outcome isn’t the production’s primary goal but is one it keeps in mind. “The whole point of turning ‘The Challenge’ into an international competition show was to showcase these locations while also reaching a new or different audience,” he says. Host T.J. Lavin says Thailand delivered some of the most memorable moments he has filmed for the show, from a season-opening challenge staged in downtown Bangkok to the daily rhythms of life in the country. “It was one of the most incredible and fun places that I’ve ever been,” Lavin says. “Not to mention, foot massages on the daily were amazing.” He says the humidity added real physical difficulty to the competition, thickening the air enough that “even some of the easiest tasks become difficult.” Thailand’s locations are also central to “Inherit,” the horror feature set to premiere as a gala presentation at the Toronto Film Festival . Director Banjong Pisanthanakun says finding the right physical spaces shapes his films as much as the scripts do. For “Inherit,” he says the main family house “actually combined three real locations plus a sound stage to create a single location that matched the exact mood we wanted.” Pisanthanakun says Thailand’s horror tradition, which he calls part of the culture’s “modern cultural heritage,” continues to travel internationally alongside newer genres such as the family drama “How to Make Millions Before Grandma Dies” and the thriller “Bad Genius.” Star Davika Hoorne, who plays a centuries-old demon matriarch in the film, says she hopes international audiences take away more than scares. “For audiences around the world, ‘Inherit’ is more than just a horror film, it’s also a glimpse into Thai culture,” Hoorne says. “I hope people feel both the thrill and the heart, and walk away pleasantly surprised.” Several of these voices are set to share a stage in Toronto. TIFF is hosting a summit panel titled “From Scenic to Scene: How Thailand Shapes Global Cinema,” billed as an exploration of how landscape, local culture and incentives turn the country into what organizers describe as “a global story engine.” Pisanthanakun and Satrusayang are the featured guests, with Phathanavirangoon moderating and Seeprae delivering opening remarks. For TAT, the ambition extends well past any single title. Seeprae says success five years from now would mean Thailand being recognized as “a prototype destination for filmmaking,” with productions returning to explore regions beyond the familiar and the resulting tourism sustained rather than a brief moment of interest. title: Freeze Turkey! 50 Years Later, the Wild True Story Behind ‘Charlie’s Angels‘
full_text: × Skip to main content The OG Angels, from left: Jaclyn Smith, Kate Jackson and Farrah Fawcett. Illustrated by Max-o-matic; Courtesy Everett Collection Once upon a time, there were three little girls who came to Hollywood — two from Texas, the other from Alabama — to become famous. And they were each, at first, assigned very captivating roles, including a nonspeaking ghost in a vampire soap opera and a pitchwoman in shaving cream and shampoo commercials. But then along came a producer who took them away from all of that, and they went to work for him. His name was Aaron. From its debut on Sept. 22, 1976, Charlie’s Angels was a phenomenon, drawing at its peak as many as 40 million viewers an episode — a massive crowd even back then, even for an Aaron Spelling show. The general opinion was that men tuned in for the bikinis and short shorts — especially when breakout star Farrah Fawcett was wearing them — while women watched for the other clothes. A few might have even turned it on just to follow the Angels’ wacky undercover assignments. Like the time they infiltrated a Roller Derby. Or the time they infiltrated a pro football cheerleading squad. Or a beauty pageant. Or a woman’s prison. Related Stories Movies Toronto: Global Media Producers Urge Stronger Local Content Laws to Fend Off Streaming Domination General News '9/11: Reunited' Firefighter on Giuliani's Mamdani Attack: "Leave Politics Out of It" Critics hated it. “When the publicity started, there was all of this criticism leveled about the show, that it was ‘jiggle TV,’ ” recalls Spelling’s widow, Candy. “Aaron didn’t take it personally, he really didn’t. He said, ‘Oh, good — more publicity.’ “ “You have to remember that ABC was like the Fox of its time,” adds David Bianculli, a veteran television critic and a co-host of NPR’s Fresh Air . “It was the youngest, smallest network. And the idea was: How do you get an audience as fast as possible? You do it by appealing to young people with attention-getting programming.” While maybe not what anyone would call a feminist show, Charlie’s Angels did come along right when women were first being liberated on network TV. In 1974, Angie Dickinson took the title role in NBC’s Police Woman ; Lynda Carter debuted in Wonder Woman in 1975, followed by Lindsay Wagner in The Bionic Woman , a spinoff of ABC’s popular The Six Million Dollar Man , in January 1976. Charlie’s Angels would transcend them all — and still, 50 years later, stands as an odd yet enduring pop cultural force that continues to bounce and jiggle back onto screens. Drew Barrymore launched two blockbuster movies based on the show in the early aughts, while Elizabeth Banks attempted a somewhat less successful relaunch in 2019. Just this past February, Sony announced it had hired The Proposal scribe Peter Chiarelli to pen a new Angels script. Half a century since its premiere, young women — and a fair number of gay men — are still doing the iconic “Angels pose” on their social media feeds, while the show remains the subject of a million memes and TikToks. Its plotlines still get endlessly dissected by feminist scholars, critics and influencers who continue to mine its fluffy 109 episodes for the deeper meaning behind such dialogue as “Freeze, turkey!” “This wasn’t Shakespeare,” admits Jaclyn Smith, who, of course, played Kelly Garrett, one of the original Angels. “It was make-believe. And you know what? The audience needed illusion. They loved illusion. We need escapes. And Charlie’s Angels was an escape.” Clockwise from top left: Cheryl Ladd signed autographs on set during season two; Fawcett’s ubiquitous red bathing suit poster; Prince Charles visited the Angels on the Fox lot in 1977; Fawcett infiltrated a Roller Derby team in season one; Fawcett showing a bad guy her foot; a season three episode with Fawcett (second from left) in a guest star role alongside her replacement, Ladd. Illustrated by Max-o-matic; Courtesy Everett Collection; Getty Images *** Spelling was already riding a wave of success during the early 1970s, having launched a series of well-rated television films and an ABC police procedural titled The Rookies . Over the course of the next two decades, into the 1980s, he’d dominate the airwaves like no other producer, with such signature frothy fare as Fantasy Island , Hart to Hart , The Love Boat and, most notably, the blockbuster primetime soap Dynasty . With The Rookies ending in early 1976, Spelling and his producing partner Leonard Goldberg were on the hunt for a starring vehicle for Kate Jackson, who had arrived on The Rookies after a small but notable part on the early ’70s horror drama Dark Shadows . They landed on a concept titled The Alley Cats , about three gorgeous dominatrix- telegraphing detectives named Alison, Lee and Catherine (as in Al-Lee-Cat). When Spelling pitched the idea to ABC’s then-vp primetime, Barry Diller, he told Spelling, “You should be ashamed of yourself.” But when freewheeling Fred Silverman took over the network a year later, the concept got a green light, with some minor adjustments. The reconceived idea now revolved around three comely policewomen who ditch their dead-end jobs to go work as private eyes for a boss they never see. “I thought it was a terrific idea,” says Robert Wagner, now 96, who ended up partnering on the show as part of the deal Spelling and Goldberg struck with ABC. “I thought the character of Townsend hiring these three ladies — it all had great possibility.” The Alley Cats became Charlie’s Angels . Husky-voiced Jackson would play Sabrina Duncan, the trio’s wiry leader and ersatz brain; Fawcett was cast as Jill Munroe, the quintessential California beach girl, sporty and evincing a million-watt smile. Rounding out the crew was Smith as smoldering ingenue Kelly Garrett (Smith originally was cast as Sabrina, until Jackson decided the role was better for her). For the never-seen Charlie, the producers hired Oscar winner Gig Young, who lost the part when he showed up to his taping drunk; John Forsythe stepped in to voice the wolfish detective agency owner. Rounding out the cast: David Ogden Stiers as the agency’s stuffy attorney, Scott Woodville, and then, later, David Doyle as the doughy, frog-voiced comic relief, assistant John Bosley. Test audiences hated the pilot, a shambolic, overly convoluted mess about a missing heiress. ABC, convinced the show was going nowhere, dispatched it as a throwaway TV movie in March 1976. Except the telefilm proved to be a smash: 30 million people tuned in, a whopping 49 percent of viewers. The network brass was shocked, but Jackson wasn’t. “I had never heard of anything like it before. And it seemed like it might work,” she says today. “Obviously, when you start a show like that, you have no idea whether it’s going to hit or not. But I always thought it was going to be successful.” The freshman show finished its initial 1976-77 season ranked fifth in the Nielsens, a breath behind CBS’ powerhouse M*A*S*H . The Angels landed on the cover of Time , and Fawcett landed in a red bathing suit on one of the most ubiquitous posters of all time. It sold 7 million copies and helped launch a whole industry of ancillary Charlie’s Angels products — dolls, trading cards, lunch boxes, hair care sets — that raked in tens of millions of dollars. But then, disaster. Just before production on season two was scheduled to begin, Fawcett announced she was quitting the show. To this day, there isn’t complete clarity on why she decided to leave. But there is no shortage of theories. Mike Pringel, who served as Fawcett’s assistant and publicist and has written two books on Angels history, says she wanted more money, “what she was worth,” as he puts it. (Fawcett and Smith earned just $5,000 an episode that first season, while Jackson made $10,000). It’s also likely that at that point Fawcett had bigger screen ambitions (although her first film after leaving Angels was Somebody Killed Her Husband with Jeff Bridges, which was such a bomb that Hollywood nicknamed it “Somebody Killed Her Career”). Jackson, though, blames Spelling, whose onerous work schedule kept his Angels locked in a gilded cage. “He didn’t want us to leave the lot. We waited all day because he didn’t want us to meet a producer and be offered something and think we were movie stars. We sat in our trailers, hours and hours,” she says. “It didn’t have to be that way.” Smith had spied trouble brewing — she remembers Fawcett kept casually telling her that she had never actually signed her contract — but was still taken by surprise. “When we had the [first-season] wrap party, we were all like a team and having fun and talking,” she says. “She never brought it up that she was really going to carry through. I guess I thought at the last minute she was going to change her mind.” Jackson says that while there was blame “on both sides” for the split — Fawcett’s failing marriage to Lee Majors undoubtedly played a role, as did Spelling’s sometimes staggering greed — “For Aaron to want a piece of that poster …” Jackson says with disbelief, citing Spelling’s desire for a cut of Fawcett’s bathing suit image profits. “Not want it, but demand it. She wasn’t going to say yes.” Spelling responded to Fawcett’s resignation by taking her to court in a breach of contract case that was splashed all over the tabloids; it was eventually settled when Fawcett reluctantly agreed to return for six guest appearances spread out over seasons three and four. But well before all of that, Spelling knew he’d need to find an actress who could replace Fawcett in season two. He homed in on spunky Cheryl Ladd, whose most notable credit to that point had been voicing one of the band members on the kiddie cartoon Josie and the Pussycats . Ladd didn’t want the job at first. But Spelling made his pitch and Ladd ultimately signed on to play Kris Munroe, bubbly kid sister of the flown-the-coop Jill. “Trying to replace Farrah? I don’t know who’s going to be brave enough to try that,” she says, recalling how she was a wreck on the first day of shooting. “I said to myself, ‘Oh man, I hope this works.’ “ Even without Fawcett, ratings stayed high in season two, possibly because Spelling kept reducing Ladd’s wardrobe to a series of diminishing bikinis. “He really, really liked my bod,” she says, laughing. “What can I say? I mean, it’s not a terrible thing. But at the same time, I said, ‘OK, Aaron, fine. I’m fine with a bikini. But only if we’re on a beach or on a boat. You have to give me that much.’” The other Angels, though, were growing increasingly restless, and not just about the outfits. Jackson was particularly vocal in her criticism of the show’s shallow scripts, which featured plotlines about them going undercover as French maids, showgirls, lifeguards and, perhaps most infamously, prison inmates. Also, Jackson couldn’t hide her deep disappointment at Fawcett’s departure, which Ladd says she took out on her. “She wasn’t warm to me,” Ladd says. “I was hoping things would get better. But I was not her favorite. She wanted Farrah. And I think she was really pissed off that Farrah left. So she had some issues there with all that change. I just kind of did my work and was pleasant.” “Oh, boy,” Smith says when I ask about the rift between Jackson and Ladd. “It was not a relationship. It was never the camaraderie of the first three. And I love Cheryl. I think she did a great job. But it was very intimidating. Those were very difficult shoes to fill.” Jackson, for her part, sounds like she might finally be ready to bury the hatchet. “The first year was just fun,” she says. “We all got along so well. And Farrah and I had the same sense of humor. And I was just disappointed that we weren’t all going to be together another year or two or three. But it worked out fine.” *** Jackson on set for the “Circus of Terror” episode, which aired in October 1977; Tanya Roberts (left), Smith and Ladd; Ladd (left), Smith and Shelley Hack in 1979; Gene Barry with Roberts in season five’s “Hula Angels,” which aired in 1981; and David Doyle as assistant John Bosley with Hack in 1980’s “Dancin’ Angels” episode. Illustrated by Max-o-matic; Courtesy Everett Collection; Getty Images As it turned out, Fawcett wasn’t the only one with big-screen dreams. Jackson was thinking about making the jump to features as well. And she had a pretty spectacular offer, from Dustin Hoffman no less. Hoffman wanted to cast Jackson in a theatrical film about a searing divorce titled Kramer vs. Kramer , and he made assurances that she could film her part around her Angels commitment. Indeed, Kramer producers revised the film’s production schedule “either four or five times” to accommodate her Angels commitment, Jackson remembers. But each time, Spelling found a reason it wouldn’t work. “Until finally Dustin called and said, ‘He’s not going to let you do it,’ ” says Jackson. A relatively unknown actress by the name of Meryl Streep ended up getting the Kramer vs. Kramer role — and won her first Oscar for it. Jackson, not surprisingly, was devastated. “I said to myself, ‘I’ll finish the season. But that’s it. I’m leaving after this.’ I pretty much let Aaron know. He said, ‘You can’t quit. You’re fired.’ “ By that time, Spelling may have had his own reasons for letting Jackson go. By the end of the 1978-79 season, Charlie’s Angels had dropped out of the top 10, tumbling from fourth to 12th. He may have seen Jackson’s departure as a chance to revive interest in the series, an opportunity to refresh the franchise. And he could think of no better way to do that than with a big, splashy hunt for a new Angel. Indeed, he would undertake the biggest actress search since Scarlett O’Hara. Not everyone was enthusiastic. “When Kate left, it was never the same for me,” says Smith. “I adored Aaron, and I wanted to uphold my contract. But all the changing Angels … the show wasn’t as fresh. They kept thinking a new Angel would bring it. They should have concentrated more on the scripts.” Amazingly, though, Spelling’s Angel hunt actually worked, at least for a time. Some 5,000 actresses were considered amid months of hysterical media prognosticating on who would wear the invisible halo next. “Aaron loved the attention,” says Candy Spelling. Henry Winkler and Cheryl Ladd co-hosted the Emmy Awards in 1979. Fawcett, Jackson and Smith fete Aaron Spelling at a tribute for the producer. Things went south, though, when Fawcett left Charlie’s Angels right before production on season two began. Says Jackson: “When we had the [first-season] wrap party, we were all like a team and having fun. Farrah never brought it up that she was really going to carry through. I thought at the last minute she was going to change her mind.” Illustrated by Max-o-matic; Getty Images *** Among those 5,000 wannabe Angels were some then-unknown actresses with such names as Michelle Pfeiffer, Barbara Bach, Melanie Griffith, Kathie Lee Gifford and Connie Sellecca. But the one who landed the role of Tiffany Welles was a perfume model by the name of Shelley Hack. Lithe, confident and oozing breezy elegance, Hack was best known as the face of Revlon’s Charlie perfume in a series of ads in which she whirled her way through various cityscapes while being serenaded by jazz pianist Bobby Short. The show’s designer, Nolan Miller, lobbied hard for Hack, whose casting offered him a chance to ditch Jackson’s turtleneck-and-jeans sensibility for high fashion. The style in season four remains the most dazzling of the series. The problem was that the clothes proved far more interesting than the plots. That’s because Spelling’s star search — and his desire to wring it for publicity for as long as he could — meant the show’s writers had no idea who they’d be writing dialogue for as they prepared the new season. As a result, for the first 10 episodes, Hack barely spoke a word. Her Tiffany was largely a vacant, immaculately tailored mannequin serving as Townsend agency décor. Another issue: Smith and Ladd, both going through divorces, wanted more time off. Apparently having finally learned his lesson, Spelling accommodated them. But that meant the narrative approach of the show had to focus more on one Angel per episode, with the other two sidelined as window dressing. It was the complete antithesis of the show’s premise. “Aaron’s concept was three girls on the screen at all times. That was the power of our show,” Smith says. “The sisterhood dwindled.” Carrying the expectations of a ratings rebound on her slender shoulders, Hack found herself isolated — and an easy target for haters who blamed the series’ continued ratings slide on her. Recalls Candy Spelling, “I’m the one that kept saying to Aaron, ‘Shelley Hack isn’t going to work.’ She wasn’t really an actress. She was a model. And the audience didn’t like her.” Adds Ladd: “She didn’t get enough to say. And I think it was a lot for her to just jump in there. It just all started crumbling around us, and I could feel it. I felt bad for her.” Fawcett skateboarded in season one; Smith filming in Vail, Colorado; Ladd still signing autographs; the Angels joined a chain gang during season one; Spelling with Ladd, Jackson and Smith in 1978. Illustrated by Max-o-matic; Courtesy Everett Collection; Getty Images Hack rallied in the latter half of the season, with the writers finally rounding her into more of a three-dimensional character. But she was abruptly dumped toward the end of the season, anyway, with three episodes still left to film. She was not happy about it and wasn’t shy about saying so in public. “I feel like I’ve been sunbathing on Three Mile Island,” she told People after the sacking was announced. “I met her and we talked about it,” Jackson recalls. “She said it felt personal. There’d be some event and the three of them were invited, but they sat her behind a big concrete post or something. She’s really smart and funny. There was no reason to treat her that badly.” Another Angel casting call was launched. This one would be quicker — only 2,000 considered. The winner this time was Tanya Roberts, a former Clairol and Ultra Brite model whom Spelling once again squeezed into ever-more-microscopic bikinis. Roberts proved to be a hurricane in heels. “She was a pistol,” Ladd says. “She had a foul mouth and would just say the most outrageous crap.” But she wasn’t Farrah. Or Kate. Or even Cheryl. By 1981, the show’s novelty had also largely worn off and the culture had mostly moved on. “When you think about its structure, the Angels were still responsible to this unseen pimp-like boss who would send them off on an assignment that would require at least one of them to be a prostitute or a porn star or a showgirl,” Fresh Air ‘s TV critic Bianculli recontextualizes the series. “It was at least equally exploitation as it was power.” Whatever it was, by the end of season five, the show fell to 59th in the ratings — out of 65. ABC canceled it, sending the Angels to network TV heaven (also known as syndicated reruns). “It had lost the magic,” Smith says wistfully. “But the magic at first was pretty amazing and pretty special.” And, it turns out, pretty durable, too. Spelling is gone — he died in 2006 — and so, of course, is Fawcett, who died three years later, as well as Roberts, who died in 2021. Weirdly, though, the show they and all the other Angels made together a half century ago — that came to define not only their careers but the entire era — somehow keeps finding its way back to our screens in one incarnation or another. Apparently, as so many polyester-clad bad guys discovered on ABC all those decades ago, Angels can’t be killed. Jaclyn Smith, Farrah Fawcett and Kate Jackson. Illustrated by Max-o-matic; Courtesy Everett Collection This story appeared in the Sept. 9 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine.

title: Venice Film Festival Takeaways: Malkovich Storms the Oscar Race, Political Movies Dominate Buzz and More
full_text: Sep 11, 2026 6:00am PT Venice Film Festival Takeaways: Malkovich Storms the Oscar Race, Political Movies Dominate Buzz and More By Rebecca Rubin Plus Icon Rebecca Rubin Senior Film and Media Reporter rebeccaarubin Latest ‘Hawaii Five-O’ Movie in the Works From ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Director Destin Daniel Cretton 19 hours ago ‘Now You See Me’ Live Show Sets Broadway Debut 23 hours ago ‘& Juliet’ to Close on Broadway After Four Years 1 day ago See All Getty Images Is Venice still vibrating from all the rounds of applause? It’s become customary for audiences at the festival’s premieres to clap and cheer for a seeming eternity after the credits roll. (Often to the visible discomfort of the actors and filmmakers, who look like they don’t know what to do with themselves when the hurrahs rage into double digits.) Call it a Champagne (or Aperol spritz — we’re in Italy, after all) problem for stars John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell and director Martin McDonagh, whose dark comedy “Wild Horse Nine” was embraced with a rousing 13-minute standing ovation inside the Lido’s famed Palazzo del Cinema. But that didn’t turn out to be the festival’s biggest reception — later in the week, Penélope Cruz and Javier Bardem received 15.5 minutes of applause for their marriage-in-crisis drama “Bunker, and on Thursday, Gaza documentary “NAZA” was greeted with a massive 24.5 minutes, the longest of any recorded ovation at a major film festival. Related Stories 'The Whisper Man' Review: Diverting Netflix Serial Killer Chiller Doesn't Demand Much of Robert De Niro And for all the complaints that Hollywood has basically abandoned film festivals, there was no shortage of celebrities to elicit big reactions from crowds. Robert Pattinson (“Primetime”), Penélope Cruz and Javier Bardem (“Bunker”) and Oasis’ Liam and Noel Gallagher (“Don’t Look Back in Anger”) were among the boldface names hoping to turn festival kudos into awards chatter or box office plaudits. Popular on Variety As Venice wraps up and festivalgoers take their last bites of pasta and sips of spritzes, here are takeaways from the floating city. George Clooney Steals the Show Only Clooney could become the talk of the fest without even having a movie to promote. The A-lister traveled to Venice not for a new project but to receive the prestigious Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement. (If that has a familiar ring, Clooney played a movie star who accepts a career honor in Italy in last year’s “Jay Kelly.”) Indeed, Clooney was everywhere this year, making appearances at a press conference, the opening-night ceremony and a master class. He had a lot to say about the power of art in times of turmoil, the importance of free speech and the fraying state of democracy. And he found time to teach festivalgoers a new term: “There’s a great word, kakistocracy, which is a country run by the least qualified people. I think maybe we have a kakistocracy right now, but we’ll get through it.” We believe you, George! Malkovich Storms Into the Oscar Race Get ready to see a lot of Malkovich. The beloved character actor is drumming up awards buzz for “Wild Horse Nine,” in which he plays an eccentric CIA agent reflecting on his life. McDonagh has a pretty good track record of getting his actors from the Lido to the Academy Awards. Rockwell and Frances McDormand won Oscars for 2017’s “Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri,” while Colin Farrell and Brendan Gleeson were nominated for 2022’s “The Banshees of Inisherin,” both of which bowed in Venice. Recognition feels long overdue for Malkovich, whose last nomination was more than three decades ago, for 1993’s “In the Line of Fire.” Matt Damon and Tom Cruise, you might have some competition… Politics, Politics, Politics Venice artistic director Alberto Barbera wasn’t exaggerating when he called this year’s lineup “the most political ever.” The 83rd edition was packed with films about hot-button issues like right-wing media barons (“Ink”), right-wing trolls (“Musk”), conflict in the Middle East (“NAZA”) and ICE (“They’re Here”). Offscreen, it’s become de rigueur to probe actors and directors at film festivals about the state of the world — a conversation that escalated at Berlin after jury president Wim Wenders said filmmakers should “stay out of politics.” Maggie Gyllenhaal, who is presiding over the Venice jury, disagrees. At the jury press conference , she called movies “fundamentally, unavoidably political” and challenged people to “hear stories about the most corrupt, most perverse people.” Her reasoning? “It opens up the opportunity to find empathy.” A Record-Breaking Embrace Audiences, for their part, seem just fine with politics at the forefront. “NAZA,” a devastating exposé about the systems behind the Israeli military’s remote killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza, elicited the longest standing ovation in film festival history. (Or, at least since journalists began reporting on the trend.) The documentary was met with 24.5 minutes of applause, surpassing the ovation for last year’s Gaza-set drama “The Voice of Hind Rajab” and that of Guillermo Del Toro’s “Pan’s Labyrinth” at Cannes in 2006, both of which clocked in at 22 minutes. Israeli directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor are two of the four filmmakers behind 2025’s Oscar-winning doc “No Other Land.” Given the warm reception for and timeliness of “NAZA,” will the duo find themselves back in the awards conversation? Where Are the Women? Gyllenhaal may be jury president, but she’s just as confused as everyone else about the dearth of women-directed films in the main competition lineup. (She didn’t select the movies, after all.) Only two titles up for the Golden Lion — “Woman Unknown,” a drama by May el-Toukhy, and “NAZA,” with Szor co-helming — were directed by women. “I guess it’s finally become clear that men make better movies than women do,” Gyllenhaal deadpanned at her press conference. In all seriousness, though, she puts the blame on the powers that be. “There’s a systemic problem,” she said. “It’s harder for women to get films financed.” A Star Is Born Lance Oppenheim, the 30-year-old director known for non-fiction work like “Some Kind of Heaven” and HBO’s “Ren Faire,” emerged as a major talent to watch. A24’s “Primetime,” his debut feature film, was one of the buzziest of the festival, scoring an enthusiastic seven minutes of applause as audiences embraced Pattinson’s immersive performance as “To Catch a Predator” host Chris Hansen. And that was just the fanfare on the Lido. The next day in Colorado, Oppenheim and Nathan Fielder unveiled their top-secret documentary about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, titled “You Can See Everything,” which became the talk of Telluride Film Festival. It’s safe to say Oppenheim will be getting plenty of use out of his tuxedo over the next few months. Feeling Hot, Hot, Hot This year’s hottest accessory? Electronic and handheld fans. Temperatures on the Lido were sweltering , which left A-listers on the verge of overheating on the red carpet. At their respective premieres, Jack O’Connell (“Ink”) had to take off his thick Dunhill coat before blotting the moisture on his face and shirt; Parker Posey (“Wild Horse Nine”) continuously waved herself with a decorative fan while mouthing about the brutal heat during the movie’s long standing ovation; and Pattinson (“Primetime”), wearing a suave all-white suit, dabbed the sweat off his forehead with napkins before posing for a cast photo. title: Global Africa Hub at TIFF Market Seeks to Boost Visibility — and Deals — for African Filmmakers in Toronto: ‘It’s Our Moment’
full_text: Sep 11, 2026 5:55am PT Global Africa Hub at TIFF Market Seeks to Boost Visibility — and Deals — for African Filmmakers in Toronto: ‘It’s Our Moment’ By Christopher Vourlias Plus Icon Christopher Vourlias Latest Telekom Srbija’s Content Head on Blueprint for Turning Serbian Production Powerhouse Into Global Player 1 day ago Serbian Sci-Fi Epic ‘Sanctuary,’ Starring ‘The Handmaid’s Tale’s’ Nina Kiri, Acquired for U.S. Distribution (EXCLUSIVE) 1 day ago Lav Diaz on the Hunt for Truth in ‘An Entry Into the Sadness of a Portuguese Woman,’ Third Chapter of His Acclaimed Hermes Trilogy (EXCLUSIVE) 4 days ago See All Courtesy of Neon, Cannes Film Festival The first-ever Toronto film market, running as part of the Toronto Film Festival , will have a robust contingent of African filmmakers, executives and industry professionals on the ground. Producers at TIFF: The Market look to capitalize on the festival’s historically strong position as a platform for some of the continent’s most diverse and exciting talents. Charles Tremblay, who heads up the market, says the event is “is designed to build on the festival’s legacy of creating access and opportunities for global content to be discovered and relevant topics to be explored. Related Stories 'The Whisper Man' Review: Diverting Netflix Serial Killer Chiller Doesn't Demand Much of Robert De Niro “We’re excited to continue our long-standing and fruitful relationship with the African continent through a variety of market initiatives for companies and creatives,” he says. “We’re very interested in the financing, production and distribution landscape in the continent at the moment … [and] our Summit programming echoes this interest.” Popular on Variety Anchoring the activities will be the Global Africa Hub, a pavilion for African creatives sponsored by Canex Creations, the pan-African initiative launched by the African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank) to finance, support and promote Africa’s creative and cultural industries. The hub is presented in partnership with Nigerian private equity firm MBO Capital, South African genre powerhouse Gambit Films, Nigerian production outfit Narratives Entertainment, and leading Nigerian production and distribution company FilmOne. Also exhibiting will be the International Salon for Audiovisual Content (SICA), a burgeoning trade fair and business hub that takes place every year in Ivory Coast. Toronto has long been one of the international industry’s leading platforms for African cinema, and this year is proving to be no exception, with new titles from South Africa’s John Trengove (“The Smell of Apples”) and Jenna Cato Bass (“Future Tense”), as well as the latest from Nigerian mogul Mo Abudu ’s EbonyLife Films (“The Secret Lives of Baba Segi’s Wives”), among the anticipated African titles set to debut. The festival will also host the North American premiere of Nigerian directing duo Arie and Chuko Esiri’s “Clarissa,” the star-studded, Lagos-set adaptation of Virginia Woolf’s “Mrs. Dalloway” that was acquired by Neon and premiered in Cannes. For Canex Creations CEO Osahon Akpata, the inaugural TIFF bazaar offers an opportunity for the pan-African investment platform to “create a bridge” between African filmmakers and the global industry. “Access to markets remains a challenge [for African filmmakers],” Akpata tells Variety . “Navigating these markets is not always something that we’re well-prepared for, and it affects our ability to get good outcomes.” One of the ways in which the TIFF partnership looks to give filmmakers a boost is through market screenings of African titles for key North American acquisition and distribution executives. “We will do as much as we can to connect them to commercial opportunities,” says Akpata. Among the works in progress to be featured are “The Black Book 2: Old Scores,” director Editi Effiong’s sequel to his blockbuster Netflix action hit, and “I’m Coming for You,” the fiction debut of Rotterdam-winning filmmaker Cyrielle Raingou (“Le Spectre de Boko Haram”). There will also be a special buyers screening of “Muganga — The One Who Treats,” the advocacy-driven drama inspired by the true story of Nobel Peace Prize laureate Dr. Denis Mukwege, directed by Marie-Hélène Roux and co-produced by Angelina Jolie. Key executives will also be on hand for a TIFF market panel on new models for financing and distributing African film, including Canex Creation’s Akpata, Gobez Media producer Tamara Dawit, MBO capital executive director Adekunle Adebiyi and Janet Brown, COO of Tribeca Enterprises. In addition, EbonyLife’s Abudu will join production and distribution veteran Moses Babatope, of the Nile Media Entertainment Group, for a session on the global success of the Nigerian film industry. Abudu is a long-time fixture at the Toronto Intl. Film Festival, where “Baba Segi’s Wives” marks EbonyLife’s fifth selection. Commenting on the prospects for African filmmakers at TIFF: The Market, she pointed to a string of sold-out screenings for the film — an adaptation of Lola Shoneyin’s 2010 debut novel — as proof that audiences are clamoring for more African stories. “I think that gives you a clue as to the appetite for our content,” she says . “The world is beginning to appreciate us for who we are. It’s our time. title: Ben Silverman, Emmanuelle Chriqui, Keshet & More On Advisory Board Of New Platform Connecting Jewish Creators With Investors — TIFF Market
full_text: Skip to main content By Andreas Wiseman Andreas Wiseman Executive Editor, Film & International @AndreasWiseman More Stories By Andreas Zurich Summit: Edward Berger, Robbie Brenner, Oliver Berben, Janine Jackowski, Martin Moszkowicz & More Join Swiss Conference Lineup Noah Schnapp, David Mazouz & Seu Jorge Leading Thriller ‘Stealing From Pablo’; Myriad Launching For TIFF Market Odeya Rush, Annarah Cymone & Neela Jolene Join Justin Long & Iris Apatow In Killer Bee Movie ‘Stung’, Filming Wraps View All September 11, 2026 5:54am Shooq Shooq EXCLUSIVE : Former NBC Co-Chairman Ben Silverman, Micah Green (CEO of 30 West), Tanya Cohen (Co-CEO of Made by Us), actress Emmanuelle Chriqui ( Entourage ), producer Anthony Bregman ( Eternal Sunshine Of The Spotless Mind ) and Keshet International are among the advisory board members of new platform Shooq , which aims to connect Jewish creators with investors keen to accelerate Jewish storytelling. The group, overseen by veteran producers Ari Pinchot and Jonathan Rubenstein, is aiming to help finance film, TV, podcasts and digital media that “strengthen Jewish identity, combat antisemitism and bring top level Jewish stories to global audiences”. Related Stories News 'R.L. Stine's Pumpkinhead 2' Launches At TIFF Market, Details Revealed With Cassandra Peterson AKA 'Elvira Mistress Of The Dark' Joining Cast News Justin Trudeau Launching Production Company At TIFF Named after the Hebrew word for marketplace and launching this week during the Toronto Film Festival and market, the group aims to connect creators with investors, media funds, studios, foundations, philanthropists, and mission-driven funding partners. Watch on Deadline According to its founders, the platform already features narrative features, TV series, podcasts and social media video content. Funders are being sought to finance development, production and marketing with each project curated by the Shooq platform to match it with an appropriate financier. Unlike crowdfunding platforms, Shooq isn’t designed to raise or manage funds directly, but more as a matchmaking platform with funders creating profiles outlining their investment interests, requirements, preferred genres, funding ranges, and areas of focus. When a project aligns with those criteria, Shooq facilitates a direct introduction between the creators and the potential funder. Any investment or grant discussions take place directly between the parties. Funders can also showcase their own projects for additional funding. According to the founders, the site already features funders from the investment and philanthropic arenas. Shooq is also offering funders access to industry consultants and “optional reporting tools and impact metrics for mission-driven funders seeking to measure their project’s cultural and social outcomes”. Participation is free and funders can participate anonymously, depending on their preference. Founders Pinchot and Rubenstein produced the Roast of Anti-Semitism comedy show in LA and run the Jewish Writers Institute with the Maimonides Fund. “Great stories shape culture,” said Pinchot. “Many investors and philanthropists have been eager to support meaningful [Jewish] media but lacked both a trusted way to curate projects and an efficient mechanism and/or the means to fully finance them. Shooq is the solution.” Jonathan Rubenstein added: “We can’t afford to keep competing with one another for the same limited resources. We need to come together under one roof, pool our resources, and give our best [Jewish] storytellers the support they need to get impactful projects made to reach audiences around the world. That is what Shooq is designed to do.” ‘Practical Magic 2’ Weaves $3.5 Million In Thursday Previews Trudeau Company; Reviews For ‘Being Heumann’, ‘The Housewife’; Photos Netflix Cancels Josh Duhamel-Minka Kelly Series After Two Seasons ‘Muppet Show’ Special Got Viewership & Emmys – Where’s The Disney+ Series Order? title: Toronto: Global Media Producers Urge Stronger Local Content Laws to Fend Off Streaming Domination
full_text: × Skip to main content By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All September 11, 2026 5:48am CEO Neal Mohan speaks onstage during the YouTube Brandcast event at Lincoln Center on May 13, 2026, in New York City. Noam Galai/Getty Images for YouTube A coalition of international media organizations has urged governments to support local producers against the “ubiquity of global streaming services” that puts commissions for diverse storytelling at risk. The call, issued at the Toronto Film Festival , comes as countries internationally have urged politicians to compel foreign streaming platforms to subsidize local media production as Netflix , Amazon and YouTube reshape the global film and TV markets. “Streaming has upended the way content gets commissioned, produced and seen, but domestic policies have not kept pace,” Reynolds Mastin, president and CEO of the Canadian Media Producers Association, representing indie producers, said in a statement that comes as TIFF kicked into gear on Friday. Related Stories Movies Toronto: Ex-Prime Minister Justin Trudeau Launches Film, TV Production Banner Hope & Hard Work Lifestyle Toronto's Best Hotel Lobbies “Canada, like so many countries around the world, needs updated laws and regulations for the digital world, and we each look to our respective governments to stand up for our cultural sovereignty,” he added. The 23 screen sector organizations signing the joint statement include European Audiovisual Production, Screen Producers Australia, Screen Producers Ireland, Animation Ireland, Swedish Film & TV Producers and AnimFrance. The call from groups representing around 750,000 workers across Canada, Australia and Europe cautioned that domestic content rules are required to shore up the production of local stories. Canadian producers recently repeated a call on the government in Ottawa to restore plans to force American companies to help subsidize domestic film and TV production as part of the larger cross-border tariffs and trade war with the U.S. The story in Europe has legacy broadcasters looking to get bigger with local government support and legislation to fend off the dominance of Netflix and Amazon on the audience side, and YouTube, Facebook and TikTok on the advertising side, or risk losing their competitive edge. The Toronto Film Festival continues through to Sept. 20. THR

title: ‘In Alaska’ Producer Tyler Hagan Wins CMPA’s Feature Producer Indiescreen Award at Toronto Film Festival
full_text: Sep 11, 2026 5:45am PT ‘In Alaska’ Producer Tyler Hagan Wins CMPA’s Feature Producer Indiescreen Award at Toronto Film Festival Anthony Cauchy scoops emerging producer award, KOTV takes TV producer award By Jennie Punter Plus Icon Jennie Punter Latest ‘The Stunt Driver’ Helmer Michael Dowse on Working With Jay Baruchel, Building a Ramp and a Rocket Car: ‘It Wasn’t for the Faint of Heart’ 1 hour ago Marie Clements on the Power of Indigenous Women’s Stories and Her Interview With Gloria Steinem: ‘We Have More in Common Than What Works To Divide Us’ (EXCLUSIVE) 1 day ago Toronto’s Indigenous Film and Industry Slates Aim to Grow Audiences and Spark Biz by Reflecting the Diversity of Global Screen Culture 1 day ago See All L-R: Tyler Hagan (Experimental Forest Films), Louis Morissette (KOTV), Anthony Cauchy (Locomotive Media) Tyler Hagan of Experimental Forest Films has won the Canadian Media Producers Association ’s (CMPA) 2026 Feature Film Producer Indiescreen Award. The plaudit was announced Sept. 10 at the Indiescreen Awards, held at a packed industry event and ceremony at the Sutton Place Hotel on the opening evening of the 51st Toronto Film Festival . The award, which recognizes a producer’s filmmaking accomplishments over the course of their career, comes with a C$20,000 (US$14,461) cash prize and is presented in partnership with Telefilm Canada . Related Stories 'The Whisper Man' Review: Diverting Netflix Serial Killer Chiller Doesn't Demand Much of Robert De Niro Recognized by the jury for his dedication to mentorship, sustainable production and community-building, as well as his passionate advocacy for emerging and underrepresented filmmakers, Hagan elevates exciting new Canadian cinema artists by nurturing talent and presenting their films at prestigious international festivals and markets. Popular on Variety Hagan’s most recent producing credits include “In Alaska” and “Seventeen,” both of which are premiering at this year’s Toronto Film Festival. He was the recipient of the Kevin Tierney Emerging Producer Indiescreen Award in 2022 for “Until The Branches Bend.” Anthony Cauchy (Locomotive Media) scooped the CMPA’s 2026 Kevin Tierney Emerging Producer Indiescreen Award, which recognizes the impressive potential of an up-and-coming producer and comes with a C$10,000 prize (US$7,230). Cauchy was recognized for his ambition in bringing French-language storytelling with impressive craft and production value to Western Canada. Through “Surf Bay, Côte Ouest,” the first francophone series filmed in British Columbia, the Vancouver-based producer showcases strong storytelling instincts and a drive to create Canadian work that crosses linguistic and regional boundaries. KOTV, headed by president Louis Morissette, took the CMPA’s 2026 TV Producer Indiescreen Award. Founded in 2011, the Quebec-based company was recognized for the depth and versatility of its body of work, which spans English and French-language productions across an array of genres and formats. “Plan B,” an innovative psychological drama starring Patrick J. Adams that has run multiple seasons and been successfully adapted for English-language audiences, was cited as a testament to that creative ambition. Morissette accepted the award and $20,000 (US$14,461) prize, which was presented in partnership with the Canada Media Fund. “At a time when cultural sovereignty has never mattered more, this year’s Indiescreen Award winners are seizing the moment,” CMPA President and CEO Reynolds Mastin said. “Each winner represents what makes Canadian independent production so exciting right now, from ambition and versatility to a willingness to push Canadian stories further than ever before. Thank you for reminding us of what we’re fighting for at this critical moment in our nation’s history.” The award winners were selected by three national juries, chaired by last year’s winners. The CMPA is the country’s leading member-based advocacy organization for independent producers. title: ‘9/11: Reunited’ Firefighter on Giuliani’s Mamdani Attack: “Leave Politics Out of It”
full_text: × Skip to main content By Seth Abramovitch Plus Icon Seth Abramovitch Senior Writer SethAbramovitch Follow Sign Up View All September 11, 2026 5:45am Bill Spade and his wife during their reunion with Carol D'Allara in 9/11 Reunited. National Geographic/Virginia Sherwood Bill Spade, one of the first responders featured in National Geographic ‘s new docuseries 9/11 : Reunited , has a message for those seeking to turn today’s 25th anniversary commemoration into a political battle: “Leave politics out of it.” Spade, the only member of Staten Island’s FDNY Rescue Company 5 crew to return home on Sept. 11, 2001, spoke to The Hollywood Reporter after former New York Mayor Rudy Giuliani called on current Mayor Zohran Mamdani to stay away from the ceremony at Ground Zero. “As firefighters, we always got a call, and if it was a fire, we responded into a building,” Spade says. “Most of the time, you couldn’t see your hand in front of your face, and we were searching for victims and survivors. We never asked the color of their skin, their nationality, their beliefs or anything like that, political affiliations. We just went in and tried to save a life and help people.” Related Stories TV 9/11 Programming Guide: Everything Airing and Streaming for the 25th Anniversary Movies Six Movies Show How Hollywood Has Grappled With 9/11 “The same thing on 9/11,” he continues. “You didn’t know who you were saving or who you were helping, and it wouldn’t have mattered anyway. You were just trying to help people.” Giuliani, who led New York during the attacks, said during a Newsmax appearance that there was “no question” Mamdani should skip the commemoration and that his attendance offended him. He also drew a connection between the Muslim mayor’s faith and the ideology of the 9/11 hijackers, claiming Mamdani was concealing a desire to make Islam the country’s dominant religion. Mamdani, New York’s first Muslim mayor, has confirmed that he will attend the ceremony and other anniversary events. He has said the focus should remain on the families “whose loved ones were stolen from them 25 years ago” and the first responders who tried to save them. “I just try to stay out of politics with it and keep it as a day of memorializing all 2,977 people,” Spade continues. “They were killed. They didn’t die. They were killed. So leave it for a day of remembering all those people, and let’s leave politics out of it.” Spade will not be at Ground Zero on Friday. He traditionally leaves the ceremony to the victims’ families and instead accepts speaking engagements elsewhere, often accompanied by his wife and sons. This year, he will participate in a firefighters’ memorial in Coppell, Texas, before appearing in Behind the Lines: A 9/11 Story , a touring stage production in which he recounts his experience alongside Army veteran Jaymes Poling and trumpeter Dominick Farinacci. In the three-part 9/11: Reunited , survivors are brought together with people whose lives became bound to theirs during the attacks. For Spade, participating offered the chance to complete something he had wanted to do for nearly 25 years: tell the sons of NYPD Emergency Service Unit officer John D’Allara about their father’s final moments. Spade and D’Allara met in the darkness inside the North Tower, where they worked together to help trapped civilians escape. Although they knew each other for only about half an hour, the two men spoke about their wives and young sons as the catastrophe unfolded around them. D’Allara was killed when the tower collapsed. Spade met D’Allara’s widow, Carol, several years later and told her what had happened, but her sons were still young. In 9/11: Reunited , he finally sits down with the now-adult brothers and recounts the conversation he shared with their father. “It was something I felt I had to do,” Spade says. “It was always lingering in my mind that I wanted to tell them about the last moments of their dad.” The meeting, he says, “lifted” a weight he had carried for decades. D’Allara’s eldest son, John, became a Marine reservist and a nurse, while his younger son, Nicholas, followed his father into the New York Police Department. Spade has told his own story at least 500 times, including during more than 300 walking tours. He now volunteers as a docent at the National September 11 Memorial & Museum, where he also speaks to graduating FDNY recruits and teachers developing classroom curricula. His two sons attended New York public schools, but Spade says their formal observance of the attacks seldom extended beyond a moment of silence. “That really bothered me, that we can’t do more in our schools than have a moment of silence,” he says. With a growing portion of the population born after the attacks, Spade believes preserving the individual stories has become more urgent. Spade says he experienced survivor’s guilt only briefly, reasoning that although he missed the men of Rescue 5, he would have missed his family even more had he died. For years, however, he had the same recurring dream. “I was in a school, and they were outside playing, all those guys,” he recalls. “I would always think, ‘Hey, I want to be outside with them playing and not here in the school.'” Then one night, his friend Mike Fiore, one of the Rescue 5 firefighters killed that day, approached the window. “He gives me the thumbs-up, like, ‘We’re okay,'” Spade says. “Since then, I’ve never had that dream. I kind of realized to move on and that they are okay.” 9/11: Reunited is streaming on Disney+ and Hulu. THR

title: New Zealand Set to Unveil Tri-Nation Indigenous Co-Production Initiative at Toronto (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Sep 11, 2026 5:45am PT New Zealand Set to Unveil Tri-Nation Indigenous Co-Production Initiative at Toronto (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest New Zealand Set to Unveil Tri-Nation Indigenous Co-Production Initiative at Toronto (EXCLUSIVE) 31 minutes ago Oscars: Singapore Selects Anthony Chen’s ‘We Are All Strangers’ for International Feature Race 4 hours ago San Sebastian Competition Title ‘Border’ Boards Reel Suspects for Global Sales (EXCLUSIVE) 6 hours ago See All New Zealand Film Commission New Zealand is set to announce a first-of-its-kind Indigenous co-production initiative at the Toronto Film Festival , New Zealand Film Commission CEO Annie Murray tells Variety . The pact will bring together Māori filmmakers from New Zealand, Aboriginal filmmakers from Australia and Indigenous Canadian filmmakers in a program of collaborative storytelling that none of the three countries could mount alone. Related Stories 'The Whisper Man' Review: Diverting Netflix Serial Killer Chiller Doesn't Demand Much of Robert De Niro “They’re not beginning filmmakers, these are mid-career filmmakers who will collaborate together on stories, working in wānanga, we call them, but very intensive workshops together in each country,” Murray says. Popular on Variety The announcement is expected on Saturday, the same day NZFC head of funding Ainsley Gardiner — a filmmaker and Oscar nominee who served as a co-producer on the first Indigenous Canada-New Zealand co-production, “Night Raiders” (2021) — participates in the From Pitch to Partner: Global Co-Production Showcase alongside reps from Telefilm Canada and Eurimages. For Murray, the initiative reflects a clear creative principle. “The real base of successful co-production is a shared creative purpose,” she says. “A strong base of mutual trust, creative alignment — it’s about creating something together that neither party could do on their own.” New Zealand arrives at TIFF with three projects spanning a wide range of scale and approach. Debut feature “God Bless You, Mr. Kopu,” from filmmaker Alex Liu, is presented by Murray as evidence of a new generation of confident, culturally specific New Zealand voices. “What it gives you is a really unique take on modern New Zealand through a cultural lens,” she says. “It shows you very clearly on screen how super diverse New Zealand is culturally.” “Man of Valor,” directed by Tearepa Kahi and screening as part of TIFF: The Market, follows Māori World War II hero Sgt. Haane during the Battle of Takrouna in Tunisia. Murray points to the film’s authenticity as the source of its power. “It works because it’s authentic,” she says, “and authenticity resonates locally and internationally.” The third project, “ Tenzing ,“ which tells the story of how Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay first reached the summit of Mount Everest, represents the international co-production end of the spectrum, produced through New Zealand’s screen production rebate and filmed across multiple countries. Across all three, Murray sees a common thread: the projects most likely to travel are those most confident in their point of origin. “The strongest stories come from a cultural confidence and a cultural pride,” she says, “and you find that in New Zealand.” On the policy front, NZFC’s recent changes to the New Zealand Screen Production Rebate are generating early traction. The minimum qualifying spend threshold for the 20% cash rebate was reduced from NZ$15 million ($8.7 million) to NZ$4 million ($2.3 million) — opening the incentive to independent and mid-budget productions that had previously found New Zealand out of reach. Murray says the first qualifying project under the new settings has already been secured, with others in advanced consideration. “It’s creating opportunities, too, for our actors,” she says. “These are films in the kind of anything from $15 million to $30 million U.S. dollars that wouldn’t have the budget to bring everybody in with them that the bigger-budget productions can do, so they are looking to source locally.” Murray frames New Zealand’s broader international appeal in terms that go beyond logistics and locations. “We have a way of doing business that is very inclusive, and celebrates diversity, and a warmth that makes it a really, really fantastic place to make creative works,” she says. “They always want to come back to do more.” ‘Shark Tank India’ Sets Season 6 With Parrot Campaign on SonyLIV (EXCLUSIVE) Hansal Mehta, Siddharth Bodke on ‘Scam 2010’ as First Look Unveiled for SonyLIV Series: ‘A Story About Ambition, Influence and Arrogance’ (EXCLUSIVE) Loading comments... title: Justin Trudeau Launching Production Company At TIFF
