The pair will officially launch the company at this year’s Toronto Film Festival. They will be repped by 3 Arts. In their official announcement, Trudeau and Telford have described the company as a “multidisciplinary media and entertainment enterprise dedicated to developing and producing engaging stories across film, television, audio and live experiences.” Related Stories Festivals John Trengove's 'The Smell Of Apples' Sells To France Ahead Of TIFF Debut Festivals Toronto Film Festival 2026: Read All Of Deadline's Reviews The company is currently developing a slate of projects, including an adaptation of Perry Chafe’s Closer by Sea, from writer and producer Perry Chafe ( Republic of Doyle). POWER MOVES by Leesa Ronald – Series A sharp, witty rivals-to-lovers romantic comedy set in the high-stakes world of politics and media. Ambitious political adviser Millsy Hatton is focused on getting her boss re-elected—until persistent journalist Archie Cohen threatens to derail both her campaign strategy and carefully controlled life. title: ‘Krux’ Director Tony Vahl Combines Practical Magic With Post-WWII Taboo: ‘A Belief Can Help You – or It Can Destroy You”
full_text: Sep 11, 2026 5:33am PT ‘Krux’ Director Tony Vahl Combines Practical Magic With Post-WWII Taboo: ‘A Belief Can Help You – or It Can Destroy You” By Marta Balaga Plus Icon Marta Balaga Latest ‘Krux’ Director Tony Vahl Combines Practical Magic With Post-WWII Taboo: ‘A Belief Can Help You – or It Can Destroy You” 31 minutes ago ‘Viva Carmen’ Reveals Clip Featuring Singer Silvia Pérez Cruz – and Brand New Song – Ahead of North American Premiere at TIFF (EXCLUSIVE) 2 hours ago Venice Final Cut Winner Machérie Ekwa Bahango on ‘Madi Makambu’ and Why She Wants Congo to Be Seen: ‘We’re a Great Nation That Needs to Write Its Own History’ 3 hours ago See All 'Krux' ©Lucasz_Bak The “Practical Magic 2” press tour might be taking over the world, but Tony Vahl ’s impressive feature debut “ Krux ” also finds space for the supernatural. Set in the final days of the WWII and premiering at TIFF and San Sebastián, it portrays a German village waiting for the inevitable: the arrival of Soviet troops. Some of its inhabitants look for ominous signs and listen to prophecies. Others don’t want to wait for a destiny they believe would be worse than death. Related Stories 'The Whisper Man' Review: Diverting Netflix Serial Killer Chiller Doesn't Demand Much of Robert De Niro “My grandmother was very superstitious. She used to tell me that you shouldn’t hang laundry on New Year’s Eve because someone might then hang themselves. I was really fascinated by this,” Vahl tells Variety . Popular on Variety “In the film, the priest has his religion. The mayor – his Nazi cult. People always need something they can hold onto. A belief is such a powerful thing. It can help you – or it can destroy you.” While Vahl leaves certain things unsaid – “I didn’t want to say ‘Russians’ or limit it to just one nation” – the fear is real. “There’s something in the air and you can’t define it,” she says. “When I was little, I would go to the riverbank with my grandmother. At that time, people didn’t talk much about the war. But my grandmother was different. She told me that in the old days, corpses would float down the river. Then she said: ‘People would go in the water.’ I didn’t understand what it meant. It sounded like a fairy tale – and a horror movie. But I remember how it made me feel. It never left me.” As the Third Reich collapsed, mass suicides claimed the lives of thousands of Germans. For the longest time, nobody talked about it. “It was a taboo. Then, about 10 years ago, Florian Huber wrote about it [in ‘Promise Me You’ll Shoot Yourself’]. I realized: ‘Oh, it’s not a unique story. It was happening all over Germany’.” In the film, starring Jella Haase, Frida-Lovisa Hamann, Clemens Schick and Lukas Miko, mass panic ensues and the unthinkable happens. “I would ask myself: ‘How could parents kill their own children?’ But they really believed that the future would bring nothing good,” says Vahl. “I wanted to find an ethical way to tell this story. If I’m being honest, all my movies are about death, but I didn’t want to exploit it. I wanted to keep certain things in the shadows because our imagination can make things even more terrifying.” Interestingly enough, Vahl doesn’t care much for war movies. “I’m not a fan, and we have a lot of them in Germany. I never wanted to make a typical war movie with explosions and soldiers. I studied psychology, so I’m more interested in people’s mentality and how we operate in extreme situations. This film is not a historical lesson, but rather a story about humanity and morality.” Keeping this in mind, she set out to uncover lesser-known secrets from that time. Just like the so-called “steel helmet wedding” (pictured) where a helmet stood in for the absent – or dead – groom. “It really happened, even though there aren’t many photos left,” she says. “I have so much respect for history and at the beginning, I focused on that more. But I’m also a big genre fan and yes, I like having some secrets. These characters have no backstories, and things just keep getting darker, like a spiral.” “I’m a big Steve McQueen fan and he used to talk about ‘body cinema’. You feel it in your gut. That was my main approach, too. I know this movie isn’t easy to watch, but I wanted to leave people with the same feeling I had after ‘Hunger,’ ‘White Ribbon’ or even ‘ The Zone of Interest .’ You are asking yourself: ‘What is this film doing to me’?” Fittingly enough, “The Zone of Interest” producer Ewa Puszczyńska is also behind “Krux” – as are Martina Haubrich, Claudia Schröter and Peter Hartwig. A Cala Filmproduktion, Extreme Emotions and Kineo Film production, it’s sold by Global Constellation. Vahl still did her research, however. For over a year. “I was always in the library, but it wasn’t easy to find information about that time. Then, I read Ian Kershaw’s ‘The End: Hitler’s Germany, 1944 – 45’ and he described the Germans as ‘dead inside’,” she says. “They didn’t question these things because they were brainwashed. There was this death cult, this hero cult. They had odd words like kadavergehorsam , which means ‘cadaver-like obedience’. The government, or the state, trained people to be without will, without a body, and without the freedom to ask questions.” She adds: “This is what happens in dictatorships. For some people, it’s easier – at least they have someone to follow. They need this kind of leadership. It happens again and again, and now we have the same situation in Germany.” Just before the interview, the far-right party AfD [Alternative für Deutschland] won big in German regional election. “It makes me really nervous,” she admits. “There’s a nice quote from Ingeborg Bachmann: ‘History teaches but has no pupils’.” Hansal Mehta, Siddharth Bodke on ‘Scam 2010’ as First Look Unveiled for SonyLIV Series: ‘A Story About Ambition, Influence and Arrogance’ (EXCLUSIVE) ‘Shark Tank India’ Sets Season 6 With Parrot Campaign on SonyLIV (EXCLUSIVE) Loading comments... Hope & Hard Work, to be run alongside co-founder Katie Telford, also unveiled a film and TV scripted and unscripted slate with a focus on Canadian stories for global export. “At a time when the world can feel increasingly divided, we believe in the power of great storytelling to bring people closer,” Trudeau and Telford said in a joint statement. title: With ‘Trash Mountain,’ Caleb Hearon Becomes Your New Favorite Indie Darling
full_text: × Skip to main content By Mia Galuppo Plus Icon Mia Galuppo Senior Entertainment Reporter miagaluppo Follow Sign Up View All September 11, 2026 5:00am Caleb Hearon Sandy Honig Caleb Hearon grew up in a small town in rural Missouri with a population under 10,000. It’s the kind of locale that can — especially for a young queer person — leave lasting scars and simultaneously build up an enduring sense of humor. The comedian and performer has long excavated his Midwestern roots for his stand-up. Now, Hearon’s life acts as the inspiration for the TIFF -bound indie Trash Mountain , Hearon’s most personal project to date. Directed by indie vet Kris Rey, Hearon co-wrote and stars in Trash Mountain as Gavin, a gay man who lives in Chicago but is called back to his small Missouri town by his half sister — played by Zooey Deschanel — after the death of their hoarder father, each of them tasked with cleaning up the emotional and literal mess left behind. Related Stories Movies 'Being Heumann' Review: Siân Heder's Drama About the Fight for Disability Rights Strikes Familiar Notes but Gets the Inspirational Uplift Job Done Movies 'Rapinoe' Review: Doc Portrait of American Soccer Icon Is Engaging and Inspiring, if Necessarily Incomplete Several years ago, Hearon‘s own father unexpectedly died. “We had a really complicated relationship — but a beautiful one,” says Hearon. “I feel lucky that we got to a really good place before he passed.” Along with his family, Hearon, who was working in a writers’ room in Los Angeles at the time, was confronted by the not-oft-talked-about logistics that come with a loved one’s passing: locating paperwork, cleaning out homes and jumping through a seemingly endless number of bureaucratic hoops. He started writing the screenplay for Trash Mountain as a cathartic exercise: “I never thought we would honestly make a movie about it.” But after sending it to filmmaker friends Colin Trevorrow and Lilly Wachowski — who each signed on as producers — the production process began in earnest. Typical of indie filmmaking, there were years of false starts, with funding and casts periodically materializing and disappearing. Hearon has built a career that spans prestige TV ( Fargo , Mr. & Mrs. Smith ), a well-regarded podcast ( So True with Caleb Hearon ) and stand-up, with his debut special, Model Comedian , released by HBO in 2025. It was during a small break in the middle of filming The Devil Wears Prada 2 — his biggest project to date where he stars alongside Meryl Streep and Anne Hathaway — that Hearon got a call from Trevorrow saying that they finally had the money to make Trash Mountain but that they would have to pick up cameras the next month. “I was like, ‘What the hell?’ ” he recalls. “Because you’ve got so many years in your career of dreaming of scenarios like where you’re at a job, and you’re talking about me having another one.” The backbone of Trash Mountain is the relationship between Hearon’s Gavin and his sister, Abbi. It’s the kind of effortlessly funny dynamic that makes the heartaches that come with having a sibling look truly worth it. Hearon shares an agent with Deschanel at CAA, and the rep told him that the actress happened to be looking for a new project and was available during Trash Mountain ’s small — very small — production window. “I was like, ‘Look, if the job is pretending to love Zooey Deschanel, it’s gonna be like the easiest acting job in the whole world,’ ” Hearon says with a laugh. At a lunch in Los Angeles with Deschanel, Hearon remembers: “I swear to God, I said, ‘Why would you do this?’ I knew everyone was going to have to do it for like $7 and a handshake in rural Illinois in the winter.” Deschanel was sold nonetheless. Trash Mountain Courtesy of TIFF Production on Trash Mountain was only 18 days and came with all the stories you would expect from true indie filmmaking, stealing locations and chasing light. One day, filming in a local big box store, Hearon kept overhearing a loud conversation from the next aisle between who he thought were members of the crew. Unbeknownst to him, they were local shoppers trying to decide which T-shirt to buy. He remembers, “I was in the middle of the take going, ‘I’m so sorry. Can we cut? People are being really loud.’ And [director Kris Rey] was like, ‘Yeah, we couldn’t afford to shut down the place, and we have about an hour left, sorry!” Trash Mountain also marks Hearon’s first time at the top of the call sheet. “During filming, I kept joking, ‘You know what this film needs? 30 pages where you don’t see Caleb.,’” he laughs. But it was also a position he didn’t take lightly, saying, “There’s this thing I’ve learned through the years of not being number one on the call sheet where I watch the people who are, and they have so many other jobs. Everyone’s energy, everyone’s tone, everyone’s gratitude flows from the director and the leads.” For already established fans of Hearon’s comedy or for audiences watching him onscreen for the first time, Trash Mountain is the kind of discovery people travel to a film festival hoping to see. A true indie with craftsmanship and heart that is bigger (much, much bigger) than its budget. “I was acting before I was ever a presence on the internet. It’s funny because sometimes I do feel that pressure of wanting people to know that I’m an artist,” says Hearon. “I do want people to know that, sure, I have a popular podcast that I’m very fucking grateful for, and I appreciate that so much, but this is what I got into all this for.” THR

title: How ‘Obsession’ Rewrote TIFF History
full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Roxborough Plus Icon Scott Roxborough Europe Bureau Chief sroxborough Follow Sign Up View All September 11, 2026 4:30am Inde Navarrette in 'Obsession.' Focus Features/Courtesy Everett Collection There has probably never been a worse moment to open a film market in Canada. The country is locked in a grinding trade war with its largest partner and closest neighbor; tariff threats have crept from steel and lumber into the entertainment conversation, and the independent film business — the actual product on offer in Toronto this week — is in the middle of its own slow-motion restructuring. The class of buoyant new distributors who arrived at TIFF two years ago with fresh cash and big talk has thinned out considerably. Streamers are buying less and paying less. Theatrical is a coin flip. Related Stories Movies The Don of Hollywood North Takes His Final Bow Movies Toronto Builds Its One-Stop Shop And yet TIFF: The Market, which runs Sept. 10-16 at the Metro Toronto Convention Centre alongside North America’s largest film festival, opens with something no first-year market has any right to: momentum, and a founding legend. A legend called Obsession . Twelve months ago, a 25-year-old YouTube sketch comedian walked into the Royal Alexandra Theatre with a horror movie he had shot for $750,000 with a cast of unknowns. He walked out with the biggest TIFF acquisition in history — an estimated $15 million worldwide deal with Focus Features — and the film went on to gross $513 million globally, becoming the top-grossing festival pickup of all time. In fact, the story of Obsession ’s TIFF triumph actually started on the Croisette. Capstone exec Ruzanna Kegeyan — who had sold 2010 Midnight Madness breakout Insidious worldwide — ambushed TIFF programmer Peter Kuplowsky the minute he landed in Cannes. “She said, ‘Have you heard of Curry Barker ?’ Initially, I blanked,” Kuplowsky says. Then she mentioned the YouTube sketches, and a long-held theory clicked into place. “I’ve long had the belief that sketch comedy writers make terrific horror filmmakers,” he says, citing Zach Cregger applying setup-and-payoff structure to Barbarian . Kegeyan sent a rough cut; Kuplowsky watched it a week later and emailed her before it was even finished. Then came the phase no market can manufacture, only host: the whisper campaign. Nobody was screening the film. So the calls came to the programmer instead. “It was constantly, ‘How good is it? Is it this?’ ” Kuplowsky says. “And I was like, ‘Well, I’m invoking Barbarian in my note, so I think it’s as good as Barbarian .’ And they’re like, ‘What does that mean, that it’s going to make $40 million?’ And I’m like, ‘I would hope so. I think it depends on who buys it and how they release it.’ ” Days before the premiere, Jason Blum, Weapons producer Roy Lee and Paranormal Activity producer Steven Schneider preemptively greenlit Barker’s follow-up project, Anything but Ghosts , alongside Divide/Conquer’s Adam Hendricks and Greg Gilreath. In hindsight, it was the best marketing spend of the festival: three of horror’s shrewdest operators publicly betting on a filmmaker whose movie no one had seen. By the time Obsession made it to TIFF, the buzz on social media had become deafening. “I remember coming out onstage for the screening, and there were people in the audience that were already chanting Curry Barker’s name,” Kuplowsky says. “Then TIFF Next Wave came out and read their introduction, describing why they connected to this film. And I pointed to them and said, ‘Buyers, this is your audience. Pay attention.’ ” Blum sprinted in during the preshow. Kuplowsky stood at the back the whole time, watching the crowd more than the film. “So electric. Every moment was working. The big jump scares got everyone out of their seat.” Christian Mercuri of Capstone, which financed the film, had felt it in the room. “You can tell during the screening,” he says. “And then — it’s not that we said 100 percent we’re selling it. We had to sit with everybody that was interested and determine that that was the right path. It was a couple of days of negotiations, and then we felt we had the right partner.” Barker’s team spent the next 24 hours in meetings, landing at roughly 1 a.m. Sunday on Focus, which beat A24 and Neon largely on the strength of a global distribution apparatus its rivals don’t have. CAA and Capstone closed it. Obsession was not a triumph of the traditional system. It was a triumph around it. The film cost less than a studio spends on a trailer, was made by a director whose audience was built for free on YouTube, and was launched by buzz, word-of-mouth and the magic of a Midnight Madness crowd. At a time when the traditional indie model — established IP, star-driven packaging, presales stitched together territory by territory — looks shaky, Obsession offers an alternative. The lesson of Obsession , Mercuri says, is to bet on “original content, original ideas and strategies that “push the envelope and take risks. As an industry, it’s sort of our responsibility to listen to some new voices, not always do the same old, same old. The core of it is original fare.” Nobody expects this week to turn a $750,000 negative into $513 million. That was never the bet. The bet is that what happened in the Royal Alexandra last year — a room full of professionals watching a debut feature work, in real time, on an audience — is worth building a market around. Not because it can be repeated on schedule, but because it proved the thing everyone had started to doubt: that an original idea, made cheap and launched smart, can still detonate. A market has to be built on something. Worse foundations have held. THR

title: The Don of Hollywood North Takes His Final Bow
full_text: × Skip to main content By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All September 11, 2026 4:00am 'The Martini Shot — 50 Years of Hits, Hustle & Hollywood North' Courtesy of Don Carmody Having racked up 130-plus movie credits over a 50-year producing career, Don Carmody has long been known as the Don of Hollywood North by studio bean counters who crunched the numbers and chose to save money by shooting in Canada. Now Carmody, at 75, is ready to leave the stage — or at least Canadian film sets — with a lavish sendoff planned for the 2026 Toronto Film Festival. “The days of me freezing my ass off at 2 o’clock in the morning on a film set are behind me,” Carmody tells The Hollywood Reporter . Related Stories Movies Toronto Builds Its One-Stop Shop Movies Female-Led Producer Candid Broads Is Proud to Stand for New Voices, Impact and Representation That’s after Hollywood catapulted him to the status of its most bankable producer in Canada, as he brought over $2 billion worth of American production north by, in effect, opening the floodgates to Los Angeles runaway production, starting in the 1980s. Carmody traces his start shepherding studio films to Canada to his time matching Hollywood production values with lower budgets as a co-producer at Cinepix Film Properties, on genre fare like David Cronenberg’s Shivers (1974) and Rabid (1976) and comedies like Ivan Reitman’s summer camp romp Meatballs . “They looked good, and people didn’t go, ‘Oh, that’s a weird-looking movie’ or ‘It’s got really bad production values.’ That opened the door for me,” Carmody recalls. The studios noticed just how much Carmody put onscreen despite tight budgets. “The studios found out how little we were spending on them and asked, ‘How do you do that?’ ” he says. He also leveraged the low Canadian dollar against the American greenback and took advantage of early tax breaks. The other unseen draw for the major studios in Canada was its creatives and crews, and local actors aligned with ACTRA, the country’s performers union. “They said, ‘Well, can you do that for us?’ So I started bringing up pictures brought to me by the studios,” Carmody explains. “Canada had a large talent pool and you could count on bringing in fresh faces. And it was important to [Hollywood] producers and directors that they see people that spoke and looked American and were really good actors.” For helping make Canada Hollywood’s backlot, the studio’s top man up north is cementing his legacy at TIFF by endowing $100,000 to establish the CMPA Don Carmody International Production Mentorship Program, putting another $100,000 into creating the CFC Don Carmody Producer Residency at the late Norman Jewison’s Canadian Film Centre and doing a Sept. 13 keynote at the TIFF market. He also screened a career documentary, The Martini Shot — 50 Years of Hits, Hustle & Hollywood North , on Sept. 9 at the Hot Docs Theatre. Of course, some Hollywood directors early on likened shooting in Canada to “being sent to Siberia,” while others welcomed how the distance from Hollywood offered more creative freedom. An early convert was the late Sidney Lumet, who knew Canada from shooting select scenes for his 1977 psychological drama Equus across the U.S. border. But when Disney’s Touchstone Pictures lost a producer, they flew Carmody to New York City to meet with Lumet and ultimately start a five-picture collaboration that included titles like the erotic thriller Guilty as Sin in 1993 and the 1997 medical satire Critical Care , both of which had Toronto doubling as New York City. “[Lumet] loved everything up here, except the bagels,” recalls Carmody. In 1997, Carmody received a call from newly hired Miramax Films head of production Kevin Hyman, who offered him the 1998 Sharon Stone title The Mighty , which shot in Toronto after a tightfisted Harvey Weinstein insisted on a budget that ruled Hollywood out. “I flew down, met with Harvey and convinced him we could make the picture look good by shooting it up in Canada, and that I would be able to handle Sharon Stone,” who wasn’t happy about heading up north, he recounts. Don Carmody, courtesy of Rafy While working on The Mighty , Carmody got another call from Hyman. Carmody remembers the conversation word for word: “OK, we have another for you. It’s very tricky. These two guys from Boston wrote this script we’d like to make, and they want to make it in Boston,” which was too costly a location, he remembers. So, with Weinstein promising a greenlight if Good Will Hunting could be done in Canada, Carmody — who spent time in Boston as a young man and could muster a convincing “Southie” accent — greeted a decidedly reluctant Matt Damon and Ben Affleck as they came through airport customs in Toronto to be shown that Canada’s biggest city could double as South Boston. “I said, OK, what do you want to see first? The duck boats? Or do you want to see the Swan Pond?’ ” Carmody recalls saying to the two stars, a reference to locales in Toronto that could double for popular land and sea tourist sites in Boston. “They couldn’t believe that existed in Toronto.” As ever, keeping a lid on the movie’s budget proved key for Carmody. “Just because I’m from Boston, that would have meant nothing if we had gone way over budget, or I couldn’t deliver the proper locations on Good Will Hunting ,” he says. An Oscar trophy eventually came Carmody’s way with Rob Marshall’s Chicago in 2002, but only after Weinstein said he would not go over a $40 million budget on the musical drama. Going forward, Carmody says the attraction of the Canadian talent pool and film tax credits (which he insists need a hike in Ontario) will keep Hollywood studios and streamers shooting in Canada. If something “amazing” comes his way, he adds, he may get back into producing, but these days Carmody is looking to exploit his original IP with sequels and adaptations, which means mostly talking to lawyers. And while being a member of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences and other industry guilds, Carmody also works with their Canadian counterparts, including the Canadian Media Producers Association, representing indie producers, along with the Academy of Canadian Cinema & Television and the Canadian Film Centre. “It’s important to support the incoming and up-and-coming producers, because Canada needs its own base of well-trained and smart producers,” he says. And if he has any advice for young producers, it’s that making movies requires patience — and stamina. Asked about the most fun he ever had making a film, Carmody says: “Probably a sequel. They’re easier,” before adding, “Making a movie is like banging your head against the wall. It feels so good when it stops.” THR

title: Toronto Builds Its One-Stop Shop
full_text: × Skip to main content By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All September 11, 2026 3:45am Geoff Macnaughton Courtesy of TIFF As the Toronto Film Festival this year launches TIFF: The Market , its official bazaar for global film, TV series and immersive content, fest organizers have also rolled out an accompanying financing and co-production forum, the International Financing & Project Market (IFPM). That’s part of a bigger plan, says Geoff Macnaughton , vp market programming and theatrical and programmer of Primetime at TIFF. Macnaughton explains that offering two markets — one for film, series and immersive projects in development, and another for completed and varied media content — is intended to provide the wider industry with what it needs to survive and thrive in an increasingly global and multiplatform media business. Related Stories Movies Female-Led Producer Candid Broads Is Proud to Stand for New Voices, Impact and Representation Movies 'Being Heumann' Review: Siân Heder's Drama About the Fight for Disability Rights Strikes Familiar Notes but Gets the Inspirational Uplift Job Done The TV series showcase at TIFF includes Mike Flanagan’s Carrie , a reimagining for Prime Video of Stephen King’s classic novel; American Hostage , the psychological thriller series for MGM+; and Yaga , the Carrie-Anne Moss and Hudson Williams supernatural mystery series. The IFPM, as a cornerstone of The Market, has TIFF taking over the International Financing Forum (IFF), a co-production market that for 20 years was run by Ontario Creates during TIFF’s 11-day run. Ontario Creates remains a presenting partner of the IFPM, with Karen Thorne-Stone, president and CEO of the provincial media support agency, welcoming TIFF expanding on the success of her longtime IFF event. “Together, we look forward to creating new opportunities for Ontario and international producers to connect, finance and bring compelling projects to audiences around the world,” she says. The Hollywood Reporter spoke to Macnaughton ahead of the Toronto Film Festival about becoming both a film and talent showcase and having two content markets in its quiver. Toronto will become a market-first festival this year. How does a returning International Financing & Project Market fit into that offer to the industry? When building the market, some of the important things for us were: How do we create a future-thinking market; another question we were asking ourselves was how do we create more opportunities for producers; the third question was how do we make sure that what we’re developing on the programming side of things is as impactful as possible? And so we kind of wrapped our brains around, if we want to support producers more, do we necessarily come in and invent something completely new? Or do we work with some partners and evolve something that’s established? And Ontario Creates has had great success with their international financing forum in past years. So instead of building a market and having the international financing forum sit outside of it, we approached the leadership team there and discussed the idea of what it might look like if this fell under the overarching market umbrella. Most IFPM projects are movies, but you’ve also included six TV series and five “innovation” projects. Is that a nod to an increasingly cross-platform and digital industry? Really, the vision of the market was very much kind of a one-stop shop for global industry professionals. The other part that was really important to us was the types of projects that were presented — that it was not only a film market, but a market that welcomed those working in film series and immersive to broaden our definition of who has access, but also bring in decision-makers and creatives who are across all of those platforms. Because among indie content makers looking for elusive financing, there’s more debate on whether a project is a film or a TV series? Yeah, exactly. And in the project market, there will be a mix of all of those. For creators and IP holders, there are more options out there than there have been. But the businesses all have various challenges and opportunities. So the idea of someone developing a film that might make more sense as a series, or someone developing a series that may make more sense as a film, or the idea I’m developing something, but it has a life across these other elements — as an IP holder, I want to take full advantage of that. With most IFPM projects being films, are movies still the engine driving TIFF and the industry’s long tail? The festival is very much the welcome party phase of a film’s life and introducing it to a public audience or a press audience or an industry audience for the first time. Obviously, the films are being acquired at various stages in their development. But we’ve seen over the last years, that finished films at film festivals are not the instant acquisition they once were. Those acquisitions take time. So, instead of trying to change how the industry works, it’s more about leaning into what the industry needs. And if what the industry needs is to showcase more projects at an earlier development stage, that’s what we’re going to lean into and offer. Where once indie film producers looked to streaming platforms for financing and acquisitions, the streamers now have their own original film pipelines. Does that leave the streamers to premiere their titles at TIFF, and indie producers to look beyond Netflix to the IFPM and your Content Market to fully finance and shop their own titles? On the streamer side of things — and I can tell by the attendance numbers and what the data is telling us — the streamers are sending their acquisitions team in a big way. The acquisitions teams are utilizing festivals, and specifically TIFF, in different ways than maybe five years ago. But they’re picking up projects at earlier stages of development. You’re seeing them pick up content out of market screenings. The streamers have a big pipeline to fill, and Toronto being the audience-friendly festival and audience-friendly market, we continue to allow for that. And how are indie producers adapting? A handful of years ago, it felt like certain companies kind of took over and were the ones that were moving the needle in terms of acquisitions. And everyone else had to kind of wait until those acquisitions were done to see what remained. That’s leveled out a bit. If you look at the last few years and the types of companies that have had the biggest acquisitions out of markets, it’s a more diverse mix. Whether it’s Focus with Obsession or theatrical distributor players like Sony Pictures Classics, they’re very active. There’s a bit more of a level playing field than there was maybe just after the pandemic. That should be an encouraging sign for producers. Besides titles, the industry is also eyeing emerging talent. Back to the point about the streamers having their own content pipelines, they’re looking in markets for talent and future talent to tie to what they’re developing. The Focus example with Obsession is a good one. A company is not only acquiring Obsession and the global hit that it became, they’re also looking to work with a Curry Barker or [ Obsession star] Inde Navarrette on their next project. That’s what a lot of theatrical or streamers or distributors are doing in Toronto, because all the markets and festivals have a plethora of emerging talent that is being showcased, not only in films with official selection, but also through our development labs and different places. To those who inevitably ask why TIFF didn’t launch an official market 10 years ago, is your answer that the IFPM and the inaugural Content Market aren’t about legacy content? It’s more about what the industry needs now and into the future? Building the market was a long-gestating decision. It wasn’t something we took lightly. We took our time with it because building a market is a big step for a festival. The idea of throwing two massive, large-scale global events at the exact same time is a feat. And over the last 25 and even 50 years, TIFF has had an industry infrastructure in some way. That’s included national agencies, that’s included talent development programs, that’s included a conference. Now to become an efficient market is to put our flag in the sand and say, “We are invested in growing our support for the global screen sector,” and it allows us to be nimble to industry changes. How people watch content is always going to evolve. But the thing that stays consistent is to get a film made, to get a series made, to get an immersive project off the ground, the business side of things needs to happen. THR

title: Female-Led Producer Candid Broads Is Proud to Stand for New Voices, Impact and Representation
full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All September 11, 2026 2:00am 'Swim Sistas' film still Courtesy of Candid Broads Productions Naomie Harris narrates Swim Sistas , a short documentary directed by actress and author Catherine Joy White that was designed as a “poetic and visually rich love letter to water, sisterhood, and the resilience of Black women across generations.” Hannah Congdon’s short doc The Long Away Game tells the story of a female Afghan refugee soccer player finding a home and community in Yorkshire, England. And Julie Magnaudet’s comedic short The Contraception Fair , starring Alex Rider ‘s Ronkẹ Adékọluẹ́jọ́, Derry Girls ‘ Kathy Kiera Clarke and The Baby ‘s Amber Grappy, follows a young woman who wants to stop taking the birth control pill, only to find herself at the “Female Contraception Fair,” an imaginary place where female contraceptive methods compete for her attention and pressure her to make a choice. Related Stories Movies How 'Obsession' Rewrote TIFF History Movies The Don of Hollywood North Takes His Final Bow Three films by three female directors, backed by one female-led production company that is focused on character-driven narratives that want to surprise audiences. And that production company has one badass name: Candid Broads Productions . Founded in 2020 in London by French-British actress and producer Oriane Pick, who serves as CEO and founder, the company’s team also features producer Anaïs Ferrato. The goal, as Candid Broads says on its website, is “to bring unspoken truths from underrepresented communities to the forefront of the entertainment industry” and “ensuring diverse female representation both in front of and behind the camera.” And it does so by combining “warmth, energy, and cinematic flair” and championing emerging filmmakers. With a slate of shorts that has made waves under its belt, the production company has started to transition into feature-length filmmaking and is eyeing a move into series, while continuing to make shorts. Pick and Ferrato talked to THR about Candid Broads’ vision, its move into new areas, and why they aren’t afraid to highlight the importance and value of diversity and inclusion at a time when there has been a political backlash against them, especially in the U.S. Candid Broads Productions CEO and founder Oriane Pick Courtesy of Kim Hardy How did the company’s name come about? “We wanted to make sure to highlight that the company is really female-centric, and we didn’t want to call it ‘chick,'” Pick recalls. “But we thought ‘broads’ seemed cool. And ‘candid’ came because we’re both French, so we’re very blunt sometimes, probably a bit too much at times. But we love being honest, and we thought having ‘candid’ in there would really work. So we’re essentially the honest chicks.” The Candid Broads brand is also meant as a signal to creatives and creative partners. “There are a lot of people who are not saying things the way they are, or hiding a little bit what the reality is,” Pick tells THR . “But we say to every writer and director who works with us. It is a very tough industry. We need to have a really thick skin. We’ll get lots of nos, but then we’ll get a yes, and the yes that we’ll get will just make up for all of the nos. So, one of the reasons we were so keen on that name for the company is because we never give up. We’re always very honest about what we do, how we do it, and we take people along the journey with us on this magnificent ride.” Female-focused doesn’t mean that Candid Broads won’t do stories about men. “We like casting a bit of a wider [net],” Ferrato tells THR . “We are female-centric, but also did a short film not so long ago called Punching Bag that follows a male protagonist. It’s really all about finding distinctive voices and taking a chance on emerging writers and directors, or sometimes a duo if they’re not the same person.” Candid Broads is all about new impulses or different approaches. “It’s all about perspective for us,” explains Ferrato. “When we read a script, we [want to think], oh, we haven’t seen that before. It may be something that has been explored, but the voice of that director or writer is bringing something that feels different.” Anaïs Ferrato, courtesy of Inès Leila Hachou Courtesy of Inès Leila Hachou After all, making an impact and taking audiences outside their comfort zones is key to Candid Broads’ mission. “It’s about stories that feel uncomfortable or difficult,” Ferrato notes, adding with a laugh. “We like making things difficult for ourselves.” After all, “it’s about impact. That’s something that we’re really interested in. Whether it’s opening a conversation, breaking stigmas, or eventually contributing to some kind of change. Of course, the impact will change depending on the film. But it has to be organic. We can’t invent it. Nine times out of 10, the story either feels urgent or very personal to the creators. And that’s what we are drawn to.” Asked about the recent political backlash in the U.S. against such ideas as representation and inclusion, the Candid Broads team is unfazed. “For us, it’s really important that everyone does their duty on it, and that we all make sure that it’s part of every film,” Pick tells THR . “Whether it’s behind the camera or in front of the camera, or the kind of story that we tell, all of that needs to be cohesive. We’re obviously Caucasian women, but we’ve been telling a lot of stories through the eyes of a Black filmmaker about a Black character. Any kind of representation is really, really vital.” Bottom line: “It’s about finding that gem and pushing stories so that we really make sure that representation is not just a word,” she emphasizes. “It’s something much bigger.” Adds Ferrato: “There’s a discourse against it at the moment, but for us, it’s always been something quite simple. When you look at who traditionally has had the opportunity to tell stories and who we’ve seen traditionally on screen most of the time, it was the same people or the same type of protagonist. But how much talent and how many stories are we missing when the opportunity isn’t there? So for us, the idea is to provide that opportunity.” ‘The Contraception Fair’ film still, courtesy of Candid Broads Productions Candid Broads actually requires at least gender parity on its sets, but most of the time, it ends up with around 60 percent women without even forcing it, the duo shares. So, what does Candid Broads have on its slate? The company has recently wrapped production on its first feature film, which is also Kieran Bourne’s feature debut, the romantic drama Arthur & Clara, starring CJ Beckford and Mirren Mack. “When a filmmaker and an actress unknowingly run away to the same rural farmhouse hoping to find themselves, they discover they only needed one person to truly see them,” its synopsis reads. Speaking of debut features, the company has been casting for the coming-of-age comedy Underdogs from writer-director Fabia Martin ( The Rev , Six for Gold ). Alisha Weir ( Abigail , Matilda the Musical ) is will star in the story, told through the eyes of disillusioned but determined teens. Underdogs follows two teenage girls in foster care who find themselves on the run in a stolen ambulance in search of family and freedom – only to end up illegally competing at Crufts, the world’s largest annual dog show, held in Birmingham, England. Grappy plays a strung-out social worker who is tasked with getting the girls back home. Also on Candid Broads’ slate is the first full-length film from Amy Hodge, entitled Am I Nervous , a feature adaptation of her and the company’s short The Date, which earned writer Bethan Marlow a 2024 BAFTA Cymru Breakthrough Award nomination. The short, which starred Millie Kiss, Sinead Matthews and Precious Scott, told the story of Sasha, “a loud-mouthed 13-year-old who goes on her first date but when she gets turned on and takes charge of her own sexuality, it reveals the confusing nature of what girls are allowed to want.” The feature, which the writer and director are co-writing, is in early development with Ffilm Cymru and “follows a teenager and a grandmother as they both embark on their own journey of reclaiming their sexuality,” Ferrato says. ‘The Date’ film still, courtesy of Candid Broads Productions Courtesy of Candid Broads Productions Also in the works is Loud & Clear , the next feature written by Kieran Bourne, which Pick is producing with Alexa Waugh ( Cielo ). More shorts are also in the pipeline. Among them is the dark comedy Vag , which will also be executive produced by Slick Films. “It’s a film about vaginismus and the politics of female pleasure and dating, written and directed by Lily Britton,” shares Ferrato. “Vaginismus is a condition that we haven’t really heard about. It’s still something that is quite taboo, and we wanted to offer a much-needed representation of it when it comes to that film.” A synopsis for the short reads: “Marianne is 27. She’s successful, vibrant, and – thanks to vaginismus – unable to have penetrative sex. When a promising romance turns sour, she’s forced to explore her own pleasure – something she’s never dared to before.” Candid Broads is also in development on its first TV series, which is being written by Ali Hughes ( Dreaming Whilst Black ), but the team isn’t ready to unveil its title or plot details yet. Mischief International is co-producing it, with its founder Maria Ishak as executive producer. The Candid Broads Productions team behind the scenes of the shoot for ‘Punching Bag,’ courtesy of Inès Leila Hachou Courtesy of Inès Leila Hachou One thing is for sure. The Candid Broads team isn’t sitting on its laurels. “We’re moving into features, bridging the gap between what we know or what we believe the audience wants, but also what the industry thinks they want and the safer choices,” highlights Ferrato. “So, right now it’s about trying to see how we can push that further. And because we have a lot of projects, we want to make sure that we have enough capacity and don’t spread ourselves too thin.” Concludes Pick: “There are a lot of different things on our slate right now, which is so exciting. We love working on very different stories at different stages, so that we just keep busy, we keep learning and we keep challenging ourselves. A main thing for us is to never get bored.” THR

title: French TV Disruptor Jeremy Zag Talks Building ‘Miraculous’ Universe, Plans For A Live-Action Series & Latest On Katy Perry Animated Movie ‘Melody’
full_text: Skip to main content By Stewart Clarke Stewart Clarke More Stories By Stewart Ross Butler & Marc Evan Jackson Join Sayani Gupta In ‘Arya’ Pablo Larraín’s ‘My Sad Dead’ Trailer: “The Dead Start To Make Themselves Present” International Sales Of French TV Programs Crash To A Ten-Year Low View All September 11, 2026 2:00am Fans of Miraculous: Tales of Ladybug & Cat Noir can expect a live-action version of the animated series, its co-creator Jeremy Zag has said. Meanwhile, his studio, Zag Entertainment, is also making headway on Melody , an animated feature film with Katy Perry . Zag co-created French animated show Miraculous through Zag. He was feted as Deadline’s 2026 French TV Disruptor this week at Unifrance’s Rendez-Vous market, recognizing his work creating animated series and movies that have travelled the world. He received the accolade in the historic surroundings of the Montivilliers Abbey in Normandy, France. Ahead of being presented with the award, the animation boss sat down with Deadline to talk about his work, and tease some of what’s next. Related Stories News International Sales Of French TV Programs Crash To A Ten-Year Low News French TV In Focus: Screenings & Shows To Watch At The Unifrance Rendez-Vous Zag explained how with Miraculous and other work he always sets out to create a whole universe, spanning TV and film as well as games and merch. “I really believe in the power of a brand, and I believe that from a little drawing, you can create a giant franchise,” he said. Zag decamped to L.A. to build Miraculous into a global franchise. He took creative inspiration from U.S. superhero culture, but also learned some American business smarts to create a universe of characters. The Zag team has a raft of new superheroes ready to join Ladybug, and Zag also teased a live-action Miraculous series. “We’re going to keep the DNA of what people love about Miraculous ,” Zag said about the project. “We are moving forward now. title: BBC Stokes Anger By Curbing Cab Rides For Night Shift Workers… As Senior Managers Spend $17,000 On Taxis In Three Months
full_text: Skip to main content By Jake Kanter Jake Kanter International Investigations Editor @Jake_Kanter More Stories By Jake BBC Stokes Anger By Curbing Cab Rides For Night Shift Workers… As Senior Managers Spend $17,000 On Taxis In Three Months Pierce Brosnan Says Tom Hardy ‘MobLand’ Feud Was “Storm In A Teacup” Channel 4 To Combine Drama & Comedy Teams Under Historic Jobs Cull View All September 11, 2026 1:37am BBC boss Matt Brittin Getty EXCLUSIVE : The BBC has sparked unrest among staff with plans to slash taxi usage for night shift workers. Bosses at the UK broadcaster want to change the qualifying time for expensable cab fares, meaning employees would have to leave work 30 minutes later or start 30 minutes earlier for the BBC to foot the bill for a car journey. Bectu and the National Union of Journalists are fighting the taxi changes, which the BBC has put forward as part of its 2027 pay offer. The BBC’s improved offer of a basic 1.5% pay rise was rejected by the unions , with further talks set to take place over the coming weeks as the spectre of industrial action looms. Related Stories News 'RuPaul's Drag Race UK' Canceled By BBC Amid "Financial Pressures" News 'RuPaul's Drag Race UK All Stars' Sets Fall 2027 Global Premiere On WOW Presents Plus BBC employees are unhappy about the below-inflation pay rise, and the cab curbs have only exacerbated unease. BBC journalists, who contribute to 24-hour news coverage, are particularly exercised about the proposals, with one insider describing them as “unreasonable.” Watch on Deadline Another accused the corporation of “pissing about around the edges” as it seeks to save £500 million ($674 million) over the coming years. Critics have also raised concerns about the safety of women who need to travel to and from work at night time. A BBC spokesperson said the broadcaster is “looking at all our operating costs” as it seeks to make savings. They added: “The safety of our staff remains paramount, and the changes have been designed to bring the BBC more in line with others in the industry and reflect the greater availability of public transport, particularly in London.” The cab curbs come as the BBC recently published senior management expense claims for the first quarter of its 2025/26 financial year. The BBC’s highest-paid staff claimed more than £13,000 ($17,600) on taxi journeys in the three months from April to June 2025. This was up 6% on the same period in 2024, according to an analysis by Deadline. The expense claims were made before the BBC introduced new cost control measures in April 2026, cracking down on travel costs and other outgoings, including attending conferences, awards, and events. A spokesperson said the BBC has “strict guidelines” for taxi usage, which apply to all staff. BBC director general Matt Brittin told staff this week that he was unimpressed by some of the expense claims, which pre-dated his arrival. “When I look at it, there are some things there that don’t make any sense to me, and I wouldn’t want to happen under my watch,” he said. “We have to spend our money very carefully, and I think we’re all very conscious of that.” Brittin added that pay talks had been a “pretty difficult process for everyone” and he acknowledged that strike action was a possibility. title: Cricket Legend Virender Sehwag To Host ‘Rise And Fall’ Season 2 For Prime Video
full_text: Skip to main content By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse Cricket Legend Virender Sehwag To Host ‘Rise And Fall’ Season 2 For Prime Video Spain’s Mediapro Group To Become Imagina After Reorganization K-Drama Day Returns For Fourth Time On Rakuten Viki With Park Ji Hoon, Bae In Hyuk & More Involved View All September 10, 2026 11:25pm EXCLUSIVE: Indian cricket legend Virender Sehwag is swapping the bat and pads for a suit and microphone. The sporting superstar, known as the Sultan of Multan, has been unveiled as host for Season 2 of Rise and Fall , Prime Video India’s reality series to replace Ashnee Grover. This marks the first time he’ll front a streaming TV show. Sehwag’s role was revealed in a trailer that you can watch above. The 1-minute 44-second trailer sees him playing versions of Albert Einstein, a doctor, a teacher and a karate yellow belt in a series of vignettes before a skyscraper building flashes on screen and the retired batsman switches to a sharp suit. “In Rise and Fall , the game of up and down is going to be very twisted,” he says to camera. Related Stories News Stephen King Calls Mike Flanagan's 'Carrie' Miniseries "Brilliant" Casting Danny Huston & Sofia Black D'Elia Among 5 To Join Kristen Stewart In Prime Video's 'The Challenger' Sehwag has long been eyed as an on-screen presence thanks to his sharp wit and straight-talking style. He retired from cricket in 2015 after a glittering career in which he became one of India’s most destructive opening batsmen and the country’s vice-captain for large portions of his international career. Watch on Deadline Numerous Indian cricketers have taken the TV pathway as their careers wound down with former Test team captain Rohit Sharma recently announcing a show, Family Full House , for Sony Entertainment Television and the likes of Ajay Jadeja and Shikhar Dhawan also fronting shows. Sourav Ganguly is the current presenter of Bigg Boss Bangla , the Bengali-language version of Big Brother , which kicked off its most recent season on August 30. Rise and Fall Season 2 was announced in March after the first run became a huge hit for Amazon’s MX Player , which has since been subsumed into Prime Video. The show is a remake of the Studio Lambert format for UK network Channel 4, though that version was cancelled after one season due to low ratings. The Indian show, from Banijay Asia , has been the breakout for the format. Set across the contrasting worlds of a penthouse and the basement in the same highrise building, the game brings together 15 celebrities, who are divided into two groups, the Rulers and the Workers. While the Rulers enjoy the privileges of the penthouse, the Workers navigate the realities of the basement. Should the Rulers. Over the course of challenges, members of the Workers are able to replace Rulers in the penthouse, changing their fortunes and the tide of the game. “The love and excitement audiences showed for Rise and Fall i n its first season gave us the perfect reason to take this unique power game forward,” said Amogh Dusad, Director and Head of AVOD Content, Prime Video India. “Season 2 brings a fresh set of personalities into a format where power is always in motion, and every decision carries a consequence. “With Virender Sehwag stepping in as host, we’re bringing a whole new energy to the show; his wit, spontaneity, and fearless personality make him an exciting fit for the game. We’re excited for audiences to experience the drama, strategy and entertainment in Rise and Fall Season 2, and watch it on Prime Video for free.” Sehwag compared the gameplay to a professional match. “Cricket has taught me one thing – no match is won before the final ball, and Rise and Fall Season 2 takes that unpredictability to another level,” he said. “As a host, what excites me about this game is that there are no easy wins and no fixed positions. The biggest challenge isn’t just getting to the top but knowing how to stay there. You have to know when to attack, when to defend, and, most importantly, when to read the game before it reads you.” Deepak Dhar, Founder and Group CEO of Banijay Asia, said the “overwhelming response that Rise and Fall received in its debut season reaffirmed the strength of its unique premise, where power, strategy and human behaviour come together to create an unpredictable game.” No launch date or contestant casting as been revealed yet, but the show will stream free on Prime Video and the MX Player Android app, which is still available under a a new identity – MX Player by Prime Video. ‘Practical Magic 2’ Weaves $3.5 Million In Thursday Previews Trudeau Company; Reviews For ‘Being Heumann’, ‘The Housewife’; Photos Netflix Cancels Josh Duhamel-Minka Kelly Series After Two Seasons ‘Muppet Show’ Special Got Viewership & Emmys – Where’s The Disney+ Series Order? title: the official opening-night film
full_text: Skip to main content By Anthony D'Alessandro Anthony D'Alessandro Editorial Director/Box Office Editor @AwardsTony More Stories By Anthony ‘Practical Magic 2’ Sparks $3.5M+ In Previews On Thursday – Box Office Update The Obsession For The Next ‘Obsession’ At TIFF: Festival Hot List Includes Pics For Sale With Cynthia Erivo, Chase Infiniti, The Maras, Dave Bautista & More Netflix Unveils U.S. Market Rollout For ‘La Bola Negra’ Theatrical Release View All July 7, 2026 7:00am TIFF The Toronto Film Festival said Tuesday that Apple Original Films’ Being Heumann from Oscar-winning CODA filmmaker Siân Heder will be the opening-night film of TIFF ‘s 51st edition in the fall. In addition, two other world premieres — Prima Facie from British director Susanna White starring three-time Oscar nominee Cynthia Erivo, and The Assassin(s) from Korean filmmaker Hur Jin-ho ( A Normal Family , TIFF ’23) — have been set for this year’s TIFF, which runs September 10-20. Related Stories Festivals Details Of Toronto Film Festival’s C$23M Market Revealed: Name & Dates Set As More Heavyweight Industry Advisors Join Ahead Of 2026 Launch Below The Line 2026-27 Awards Season Calendar: Oscars, Emmys, Grammys, Guilds & More Being Heumann stars BAFTA Award nominee Ruth Madeley ( Don’t Take My Baby ) as famed disability activist Judy Heumann in what is a feature take of her bestselling memoir. Being Heumann follows Heumann as she leads more than 100 disabled people to take over the San Francisco Federal Building, kicking off a 28 day sit-in in 1977. The protestors form a tightly bound community, refusing to leave until the government enforces section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, which required all federal spaces to become accessible. Heder and Rebekah Tussing adapted the memoir. Mark Ruffalo, Dylan O’Brien, Jon Beavers, Rob Delaney, Ray Fisher and more star in the pic. David Permut, Heder, John W. Beach, Kevin Cleary and Kevin J. Walsh produce. Watch on Deadline ‘Prima Facie’ Prima Facie is the feature adaptation of the West End and Broadway play (which originally starred Jodie Comer). Erivo plays a British defense barrister who exudes enviable brilliance in navigating the ruthless and gladiatorial London courtrooms. She is formidable in her defense of men charged with sexual assault; but just as she is fast-tracking to stardom, the tide turns to crisis, and she must fight to define herself. Playwright Suzie Miller adapted her Olivier-winning and Tony-nominated play for the big screen. Deadline first told you about the project at Cannes 2025, when Embankment Films handled global sales with UTA Independent Film Group and CAA Media Finance co-representing domestic. The Assassin(s) is set in 1974 and follows the attempted assassination of Korean president Park Chung-hee on August 15 of that year — one of the most consequential days in the country’s history. Yoo Hae-jin, Park Hae-il and Lee Min-ho star. Park portrays a news editor who delves into unanswered questions surrounding the attempted assassination. Yoo is the police inspector, and Lee is a journalist both of whom witness the assassination. “We’re thrilled to open this year’s festival with Siân Heder’s inspiring follow-up to her Oscar-winning CODA ,” TIFF CEO Cameron Bailey said. “ Being Heumann features an electric performance from Ruth Madeley in the story of Judy Heumann, a world-changing advocate for accessibility. We’re also glad to reveal the news that Toronto audiences will be the first to see Cynthia Erivo in Susanna White’s searing legal drama Prima Facie , and that the South Korean power duo of director Hur Jin-ho and superstar Lee Min-ho will launch their thriller The Assassin(s) at our 51st festival. Lots more to come.” Being Heumann will debut on Thursday, September 10 at Roy Thomson Hall. Last year’s TIFF drew 700,000 attendees.
